of reach and should therefore be thought of as processual: a striving to achieve 
reassuring and confirmatory stories of the Self.
Drawing on Mitzen, 20 we argue that ontological security and the reduction 
of international anxiety are pursued as much in the writing of Otherness relative 
to recurrent coalition partners as to military opponents. Specifically, more than 
merely ‘rivals in arms’,21 France and the Anglosphere are ‘brOthers in arms’. In the 
contemporary era, France and the Anglosphere are allies, not enemies. Yet, despite 
their shared interests, analogous strategic cultures and similar world-views—as 
well as repeated participation in coalition warfare—France and the Anglosphere 
are Others. Their identities rely on a relationship with each other that is premised 
as much on relational alterity as shared values. As such, they are fully imbricated 
in each other’s storying of biographical continuity; their ontological security and 
sustained sense of Self are wrapped up in familiar distinctions with their ally. 22
France and the Anglosphere: complementary, competing and co-consti-
tutive exceptionalisms
France–Anglosphere relations exist a step back from the fraternal imbrications 
of the old Anglosphere coalition. They are, however, unique, deeply enmeshed 
and conditioning of bilateral policy possibilities. What marks out the France –
Anglosphere relationship from others (who might equally claim to be ‘brOthers 
in arms’) is that it is built upon symbiotic exceptionalisms, which are comple-
mentary, competing and co-constitutive. The countries fight together readily and 
frequently in pursuit of mutual goals due to the complementarity of their excep-
tionalist (universalist) objectives, yet they compete with each other for influence 
and ascendancy due to precisely these similar aims and understandings. They are 
also co-constitutive, relying on each other to narrate and construct a sense of Self 
in pursuit of ontological security. France and the Anglosphere are ‘brOthers in 
arms’, defined in mutual contradistinction to their allies.
US, British and Australian exceptionalisms underpin the ‘old Anglosphere 
coalition’, inspiring coalition militarism in pursuit of liberal values.23 As the junior 
coalition partner, Australia is often overlooked, despite its historical significance 
in allied campaigns and recent centrality to US, UK and French Indo-Pacific 
strategies. Australian exceptionalism is fiercely contested,24 while three principal 
themes sustain exceptionalist sentiment. First, is the powerful political mythology 
of ‘mateship’ which draws on and helps to sustain claims of egalitarianism at home

relations are those with the UK and particularly the US. For the United States—
the exceptionalist state par excellence—exceptionalism remains a powerful under -
pinning of self-understanding, an enduring motivator for military (in)action and a 
resonant component of political oratory.35  Historically, two principal dimensions 
have structured this narrative: the geographical and the ideological.36  Infamously, 
from Alexis de Tocqueville onwards, exceptionalist thinking proclaimed that 
America’s fortune was to have been blessed by divine providence—a vast, bountiful 
land, protected by two great oceans. This prosperous New W orld awaited those 
fleeing the persecutions of the Old—the whim of European autocrats and the 
hounding of the church. Exceptionalist narratives thus took shape in explicit 
juxtaposition with Europe; a sense of ideological superiority—and freedom—
was built through direct contrast, as alterity was rendered formative and produc-
tive.37  This afforded the American experiment universal significance, positioning 
the US as the last great hope for mankind. While the impact of exceptionalism 
on US foreign policy has not been linear, 38  it has led the US time and again to 
seek to shape the world in its own image—whether through benign inspiration or 
force—taking on the self-proclaimed role of leader of the free world.
Like the US, the concept of ‘French exceptionalism’ is complex and multi-
faceted.39  France’s international status has altered significantly since the eras of 
Louis XIV or Napoléon Bonaparte, but French leaders have continued to promote 
France’s ‘rank’,40 arguing that France is ‘more than a middle size power’. 41 The 
arguments put forward to underpin claims of exceptionalism have remained 
relatively constant in the post-Cold War era:42 the idea that France is ‘the homeland 
of human rights’ and, as such, has a special responsibility to protect and promote 
them; its permanent seat at the UN Security Council; its capacity to intervene 
militarily in most of the world; the fact that it is a nuclear power; its economic 
status; and its cultural influence (in particular, through the Francophonie, but also

Case selection: AUKUS
The development of AUKUS represents an urgent contemporary case-study for 
France–Anglosphere relations. The partnership’s founding constitutes an impor-

order would spectacularly, and without forewarning, shun a like-minded, reliable 
ally with mutual aims, risking their future cooperation.
Announced in September  2021, AUKUS promises cooperation between the 
US, UK and Australia in advanced military technology (such as artificial intelli-

submarines to Australia. However, AUKUS is far more than that: the partner -
ship represents the drawing of lines in the battle to influence and shape the Indo-
Pacific at a moment when China is particularly bellicose. 56  The announcement, 
therefore, is highly significant: AUKUS is designed to be at the heart of efforts to 
manage global reordering in the twenty-first century, defending liberal interna-
tional order through advanced military capability.
In the post-Cold War security environment, this is a position that has also been 
readily and repeatedly taken up by France. Playing a central role in the defence 
of liberal norms—in the fields of human rights and human protection, in partic-

deployments in Libya, Syria and Mali. In Libya, for example, assertive French 
calls to intervene created the policy embarrassment for Obama of being seen to

Notwithstanding the existence of important nuances, the overriding objectives 
of AUKUS are shared by France;58  the four states are ‘powers who share a common 
goal—to contain the growing influence of China’ and defend liberal international 
order.59  As a result, AUKUS can readily be interpreted as a paradox. On the one 
hand, the partnership symbolizes a long-term resolve to confront China, protect 
the Indo-Pacific and defend an international order built in the Anglosphere’s own 
image. On the other hand, AUKUS recklessly risked isolating the single state more 
prepared to fight for liberal international order than any other: France.
Data selection and methods: discourse analysis and elite interviews
To analyse the rationale behind AUKUS, and its impact on France –Anglosphere 
relations, two complementary methods were employed: 1) a computer-aided 
discourse analysis of key texts from French and Anglosphere political elites and 
the media; and 2) a series of semi-structured interviews with policy-makers and 
practitioners.
First, the project analysed 540  political elite and media texts from France, 
the US, UK and Australia in the ten months following the announcement of 
AUKUS (September  2021–June  2022).60  Texts were selected based on keyword 
inclusion and following Lene Hansen’s ‘model 2’ approach to data composition for 
discourse analysis:61  sources included government, opposition and media texts. 62  
Political elite texts were sourced from authorized speakers, such as state leaders, 
and foreign and defence secretaries. Parliamentary and congressional debates on 
AUKUS were also included. For media texts, data was collected from key newspa-
pers in each state, which respected broad representative partisan coverage.63  Texts 
were imported into the qualitative software NVivo for coding. The French and 
English codebooks were developed thematically and abductively, with extensive 
case knowledge allied to the inductive coding of a small (approximately 10 per 
cent) sample of the data. Two coders, one whose native language was English and 
the other French, conducted the coding of the data, applying the codebook. 64

summary_html:
Main argument: The article argues that France’s relationship with the Anglosphere, especially under the new AUKUS security partnership, is best understood through the concept of ‘brOthers in arms’—a relationship marked by simultaneous fraternity and alterity underpinned by competing but complementary exceptionalisms that shape alliance politics and ontological security narratives.

Research design: This is a qualitative, mixed-methods case study focusing on the AUKUS announcement as a critical moment in France-Anglosphere relations. It combines constructivist ontological security theory with historical foreign policy analysis to explore alliance dynamics.

Method: The study employs computer-aided discourse analysis of political and media texts alongside semi-structured elite interviews with 37 policymakers and practitioners from France, the US, UK, and Australia.

Dataset or evidence: The dataset includes 540 political elite and media texts from the four countries, collected between September 2021 and June 2022, combined with 37 qualitative interviews spanning government, military, diplomatic, and academic sectors.

Unit of analysis: The primary unit of analysis is the France–Anglosphere relationship, particularly how it manifests in discourse and elite perceptions surrounding the AUKUS pact and alliance politics.

Time period studied: The focus is on the post-AUKUS announcement period from September 2021 to June 2022, contextualized within the longer historical arc of France–Anglosphere relations.

Geographic focus: The study centers on the transnational relationships between France, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia, with broader implications for the Indo-Pacific region.

Identification strategy: The article identifies the impact and rationale of AUKUS through thematic discourse analysis and elite interviews, triangulating public political narratives with private stakeholder insights to reveal the social-constructed foundations of alliance politics.

Key findings: The authors find that despite shared strategic objectives—primarily containing China and defending liberal order—AUKUS severely damaged France’s trust in Anglosphere partners due to its secretive exclusion and submarine deal cancellation. France and the Anglosphere maintain a complex ‘brOthers in arms’ relationship, characterized by complementary yet competing exceptionalisms that simultaneously bind and divide these allies. The partnership is driven by ontological security dynamics shaped by cultural intimacy and historical narrative frameworks.

Main limitations: The research focuses primarily on discourse and elite perceptions, which may overlook structural or material considerations underpinning AUKUS. Its recency limits longitudinal analysis, and the dataset is constrained to texts and interviews available within a short post-announcement timeframe.

Why this matters for IR scholars: This study advances understanding of alliance politics beyond rationalist security frameworks by integrating ontological security and identity narratives, showing how major and middle powers manage durable yet fraught partnerships. It highlights the centrality of cultural and historical narratives in shaping strategic trust and alliance cohesion.

Why this matters for strategic infrastructure research: Given AUKUS’s significance in military technology cooperation—especially nuclear submarine development and emerging technologies—the research sheds light on the geopolitical and alliance dynamics affecting strategic defense infrastructure, technological competition, and great power order shaping in the Indo-Pacific.

title: A Neglected Region? The Strategic Value of the South Atlantic
abstract:
In March 2021, a colossal container ship named Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal, blocking one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes for almost a week. It was reported that the delay held up some $10 billion USD in global trade.Footnote1 Although an incident like this is relatively rare and does not pose a structural threat to global trade, it highlights the fragility of commercial maritime routes, and how interconnected the world’s maritime regions—also known as maritime orders—are. Of these, the Indo-Pacific and the South Atlantic are the most significant maritime orders, transporting the vast bulk of global sea freight, which notably surpasses both land and air freight by a wide margin. Yet with all the focus on the Indo-Pacific maritime regional order, the South Atlantic’s centrality to global peace and prosperity is often neglected. By “South Atlantic,” we are referring to those areas of the Atlantic Ocean between Africa and South America below the equator, and whose roughly eighty countries—including important economies like Argentina, Brazil, Nigeria, and South Africa—are part of the Global South. As the world’s other key maritime order, the South Atlantic represents an indivisible component of the three-quarters of the planet that is covered by water. It also includes two highly strategic passageways—the Panama Canal and Cape Hope—which provide, in practical terms, the only access to and from the Indian and Pacific oceans.

Recent scholarship has tangentially drawn attention to the centrality of the South Atlantic maritime order and how these regions relate to the Indo-Pacific, the nexus of contemporary great power rivalry.Footnote2 Yet as we argue in this article, the South Atlantic remains neglected at the level of grand strategy. Despite this maritime order being in its own backyard, Washington has singularly failed to provide a comprehensive policy outlook for the South Atlantic. This appears to be a glaring omission given that the stability of the South Atlantic order is more relevant than ever at a time of reemerging rival geopolitical blocs, loosely led by the United States and China.Footnote3 Moreover, the South Atlantic is an indispensable shipping route and abundant in natural resources and thus has consequences for the global economy.

Our article makes two key arguments. First, the South Atlantic not only represents a highly strategic region in its own right, but it has a tangible structural function in supporting the flows of global trade and supply chains that underpin other regional orders, particularly the pivotal Indo-Pacific. The South Atlantic’s significance derives from the globalization of shipping lanes, the region’s plentiful natural resources, and the geographical dependency of the Indo-Pacific on the Panama Canal and Cape Horn for westward shipping lanes. Increasingly significant in an era of trade wars, the South Atlantic provides an alternative geography for rerouting supply chains, supporting Western states as they engage in derisking and decoupling of their trading arrangements away from China. With the world slipping back into bloc politics, governments of the South Atlantic have so far resisted being pulled one way or another, which cements this region as a viable option for supply chain rerouting.

Second, Western states would reap benefits in rebalancing their grand strategies toward the South Atlantic. This is not about military engagement with the region, as has characterized the Western pivot toward the Indo-Pacific, but more about developing a comprehensive strategy to maintain the region as a peaceful environment. Targeted and sustainable measures such as an Atlantic-wide emphasis on multilateral engagement, promotion of regional trade, and provision of maritime security would increase the stability of the wider world order. At the same time, Western engagement with the South Atlantic should avoid exclusionary minilateral frameworks—as seen in the Indo-Pacific—so as not to undermine the West’s legitimacy as an external hegemonic actor. Despite the recent flashpoints for global security (most obviously the Ukraine war and Gaza conflict), the centrality of regional maritime orders suggests that not all threats are localized or single-ticket items.

Rather than viewing crises in isolation, Western policymakers would do better by connecting decision-making with grand strategic priorities rather than being on their back foot in responding to crises, particularly in an era where China and other adversaries are increasingly resorting to the weaponization of supply chains that concern critical commodities. Even more fundamentally, contemporary great power rivalry can be viewed through the lens of maritime orders, and herein may lie the solutions. Rather than viewing the region as a collection of weak and irrelevant economies disenfranchised by vast geographical distances, it is their very connectedness and interdependence afforded by their maritime dimension as a global shipping and infrastructure route that makes the South Atlantic so critical to the stability of the global system.

A Neglected Region? The 
Strategic Value of the 
South Atlantic
I n March 2021, a colossal container ship named Ever Given ran 
aground in the Suez Canal, blocking one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes 
for almost a week. It was reported that the delay held up some $10 billion 
USD in global trade.
1
Although an incident like this is relatively rare and does 
not pose a structural threat to global trade, it highlights the fragility of commer -
cial maritime routes, and how interconnected the world’s maritime regions—also 
known as maritime orders—are. Of these, the Indo-Pacific and the South Atlan -
tic are the most significant maritime orders, transporting the vast bulk of global 
sea freight, which notably surpasses both land and air freight by a wide margin. 
Yet with all the focus on the Indo-Pacific maritime regional order, the South 
Atlantic’s centrality to global peace and prosperity is often neglected. By 
“South Atlantic,” we are referring to those areas of the Atlantic Ocean

at the level of grand strategy. Despite this mar -

Our article makes two key arguments. First, the South Atlantic not only rep -
resents a highly strategic region in its own right, but it has a tangible structural 
function in supporting the flows of global trade and supply chains that underpin 
other regional orders, particularly the pivotal Indo-Pacific. The South Atlantic’s 
significance derives from the globalization of shipping lanes, the region’s plentiful 
natural resources, and the geographical dependency of the Indo-Pacific on the 
Panama Canal and Cape Horn for westward shipping lanes. Increasingly signifi -
cant in an era of trade wars, the South Atlantic provides an alternative geography 
for rerouting supply chains, supporting Western states as they engage in derisking 
and decoupling of their trading arrangements away from China. With the world 
slipping back into bloc politics, governments of the South Atlantic have so far 
resisted being pulled one way or another, which cements this region as a viable 
option for supply chain rerouting.
Second, Western states would reap benefits in rebalancing their grand strategies 
toward the South Atlantic. This is not about military engagement with the region, 
as has characterized the Western pivot toward the Indo-Pacific, but more 
about developing a comprehensive strategy to maintain the region as a peaceful 
environment. Targeted and sustainable measures such as an Atlantic-wide

Conceptualizing Maritime Orders
At its simplest, a maritime order can be understood as an expansive maritime 
region in which order derives from how states and the international community 
at large make legal and sustainable use of the seas and oceans therein. Maritime 
orders may be used for any of the following activities, either separately or in com -
bination: dominion, strategic maneuver, resource extraction or management, or 
most commonly, transportation.
4
Solidity and sustainability in a maritime order 
derive from a combination of relatively stable patterns of state behavior, rules 
governing claims to both maritime resources and areas, and legal mechanisms 
in place in the event of an international maritime dispute.
5
A maritime order is nevertheless constantly in flux as it is affected by develop -
ments such as military actions that shape the balance of power, localized crises, 
and geoeconomic dynamics. As such, a broader understanding of maritime 
order that acknowledges contemporary great power dynamics is pertinent. 
Indeed, scholars have referred to this era as a “maritime century,” a conceptual -
ization that takes into account that oceans and seas provide resources to states 
and enable them to project power.
6
From these waterways spring digital and phys -
ical connectivity, driving economic prosperity while bringing countries and their 
peoples together. Yet equally, a maritime order is a vehicle of threats, whether 
stemming from states or non-state actors. In today’s world, power is being

8
As well as advocating for more attention to be afforded to the South Atlantic, 
our article also reflects on the conceptual significance of maritime orders, particu -
larly salient in the context of the US-China rivalry, which has a distinctive mar -
itime dimension. Our contributions here are twofold. First, a maritime order 
needs to be conceived of  as a dispersed and distributed theater through which 
events in one place may impact security dynamics on the other side of the 
world. In a globalized world layered with interdependent supply chains and 
migration flows, regions are intrinsically interconnected and opportunities as 
well as threats travel across space, meaning that maritime-based threats in one 
region should not be seen in isolation from other regions. Second, the oceans 
matter insofar as their control can either lead to access to—or exclusion 
from—a large swath of territory or passage. Yet equally as important as states 
engaging on transnational issues are indigenous actors widely and actively parti -
cipating in managing local or regional matters. That many of the world’s low- 
lying island nations are at risk of becoming unhabitable due to rising sea levels 
linked to climate change is an existential crisis which deserves their inhabitants 
a seat at the top table of multilateral decision-making.
Neglecting the South Atlantic
In the past decade, the Indo-Pacific region—and, by extension, the Indo-Pacific 
maritime order—has attracted much attention in Western policy circles. This has 
led to a proliferation of national strategy doctrines which highlight the region’s 
importance to global order. The United States anticipated this shift by launching 
its “pivot to Asia” as early as 2011, a strategy driven by the economic imperative 
of the growing size of the Asian middle class and the geostrategic imperative of 
China’s maritime claims over contested international waters.
9
Other Western 
powers quickly followed. Germany stated in its 2020 national strategy that the 
Indo-Pacific “is becoming the key to shaping the international order in the 
21st century,”
10
while Canada argued in its 2022 strategy that this region is 
“rapidly becoming the global centre of economic dynamism and strategic chal -
lenge.”
11
During the same period, the UK highlighted the “growing importance 
of the Indo-Pacific to global prosperity and security,”
12
and France stated that 
the region is the “new driver of global growth for the past two decades” and 
“at the heart of major global challenges.”
13
NATO and the EU made similar 
references in their strategic concepts.
14

Resource Security Amidst Supply Chain W eaponization
The South Atlantic contains vast natural resources that have increased strategic 
importance as we transition into the fifth industrial revolution characterized by 
advanced technologies. It also provides energy resources for many Western 
states. Brazil is now the seventh largest producer of crude oil since the discovery 
of its offshore “pre-salt” layer in the mid-2000s and holds the second-largest crude 
oil reserves in Latin America, behind Venezuela. Most of its oil and natural gas 
production occurs offshore in the South Atlantic. Argentina is currently expand -
ing its oil and natural gas exports with the discovery of new large onshore and 
offshore reserves.
26
Commercially viable reserves in the Falklands have made 
the British territory another possible area of production.
27
On the eastern shores of the Atlantic, in the resource-rich Gulf of Guinea, 
there are four of OPEC’s twelve members: Nigeria, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, 
and the Republic of Congo. Africa is home to around 10 percent of the world’s 
conventional oil and gas resources.
28
Nigeria regularly ranks among the top 
five exporters of liquefied natural gas (LNG) worldwide,
29
while former OPEC 
member Angola has natural gas reserves on par with Brazil. Ghana and Cameroon

South Atlantic Maritime Order for Global Security
As Alfred Thayer Mahan argued in the nineteenth century, command of the seas 
is intrinsically linked to the security of maritime trade and commerce.
37
If 
regional security is challenged, the regional maritime order also is.
38
Although 
still regarded as a peripheral region, the South Atlantic maritime order connects 
the highly consequential Indian and Southern Pacific oceans, and thus constitu -
tes a central part of the sea lanes used by the United States and most of the 
world’s trading powers. British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher recognized 
this at the outbreak of the Falklands War when she declared “the strategic

Cultivating a Multilateral Regional Order
Recognizing their trading bonds and shared interests, states of the South Atlantic 
have over the years sought to build regional governance architecture. However, 
such efforts have been limited compared to other maritime orders like the Indo- 
Pacific, where ASEAN has become a dominant international player in its own 
right. Apart from the obvious challenge of enormous geographical distances 
among states across the Atlantic, other factors for why multilateral regional 
architecture has not yet emerged include structural impediments related to 
how the world’s various regions have historically been defined and constituted,
46
as well as the region’s multiple languages and geographical barriers.
47
All these 
factors make the South Atlantic difficult to comprehend in a coherent way. 
Not only would a regional governance framework go a long way to induce 
greater regional stability and economic prosperity, it would also enable South 
Atlantic states to cooperate more strategically with one another, and in turn 
wield regional influence within global institutional structures.
Early efforts at regional multilateralism highlight the complexity of the South 
Atlantic maritime order. During the 1960s, apartheid South Africa put forward a 
proposal to create a South Atlantic Treaty Organization (SATO), modeled on 
NATO, as a means to resist Soviet expansionism. Seen as an attempt to legitimize 
the apartheid regime, the project foundered. A subsequent South African proposal 
in the 1970s likewise failed, although this time opposed by Brazil on the basis that 
the Soviet Union posed no threat to South America (it was argued that the Inter- 
American Treaty of Reciprocal Assistance would suffice).
48
Although great powers 
such as the United Kingdom, and at a later stage the United States, supported these 
proposals, the 1982 Falklands War ended Argentina’s enthusiasm for SATO, and 
thus prospects for building a regional military alliance.
49
In part, the failure of SATO reflected the limits of externally imposed or exter -
nally modeled frameworks. However, even indigenous multilateral initiatives 
foundered. One of the most important of these was the South Atlantic Peace 
and Cooperation Zone (ZOPACAS) established in 1986 through a UN resol -
ution, but ultimately never fully realized over the years. Initially, ZOPACAS’ 
main objective was to keep the region nuclear weapons-free and safe from exter -
nal military interventions while maintaining the territorial integrity of its 
members.
50
Indeed, its creation and aims were partly a response to the Falklands

The Risk of Hypocrisy
Since the inception of European commercial and colonial expansionism, the 
South Atlantic has been within the Western sphere of economic and political 
influence. Although by the nineteenth century, great power dynamics privileged 
relations between the United States and European states, now understood within 
the rubric of transatlantic relations, the South Atlantic remained highly conse -
quential to the Western-led liberal international order. The Cold War triggered 
concerns for security across the South Atlantic, particularly when a select 
number of states—including Cuba and Angola—came under Soviet influence.
Nevertheless, the United States retained regional primacy throughout the 
twentieth century, even as European states in parallel underwent loss of empire 
and their influence relentlessly diminished. In its wake, decolonialization saw 
the emergence of a large number of new sovereign nation-states with their 
own political agendas and varying degrees of regional influence. Into the early

the West to secure resources and keep the area well within Western influence.

Learning the Lessons of the Exclusion T rap
Although it is tempting to conceptualize the states of the South Atlantic mari -
time order as a community, they manifest most tangibly with an even broader 
Global South identity. It is probably more accurate to conceptualize their inter -
ests as only tangentially aligned, being driven by geographical and spatial realism 
which means that security priorities are local, rather than regional or global.
60
Yet 
similar arguments are still made about the Indo-Pacific maritime order, and 
“whether this can be institutionalized.”
61
In this regard, there are lessons to be 
learned from the experience of the Indo-Pacific. One of these is that Western 
states would be wise not to replicate exclusionary strategies for the South Atlan -
tic which threaten to drive regional states into binary groupings. In particular, a 
minilateral vehicle such as AUKUS that has an Anglosphere identity could be 
potentially divisive.
62

challenges, the bloc has for many decades played a healthy hedging role in mitigat -
ing tensions between the great powers and the possibility of a regional order 
becoming bipolar.
64
In the short term, a ZOPACAS centrality may disappoint 
some Western powers insofar as it would make negotiating bilateral issues more dif -
ficult. Nevertheless, it might not only contribute to stabilizing the regional order, 
but also help to limit the impact of geopolitical turbulence more widely.
The Global South is attempting to break the vicious cycle of economic depen -
dence on the Global North. China is seeking to increase its presence in the region, 
but its soft power remains limited to providing infrastructure and selling cheap 
technology, which is not fundamentally different from the conservative approach 
taken historically by the West. Thus, a third lesson for the West is sustaining an 
already privileged role in the region through soft power initiatives such as trade 
deals, research and development (R&D) collaboration, and more generally increas -
ing regional trade, particularly in the areas of technology. Sharing the know-how 
and enabling regional powers to indigenize technology that they need—a good 
example is electric cars in Brazil—could allow the West to consolidate its legiti -
macy across the South Atlantic maritime order through engagement that provides 
more sustainable and tangible benefits to the region at large.
65
Our article has recognized the growing importance of the South Atlantic in an 
increasingly unstable world order. Although the South Atlantic has been largely 
peaceful in recent decades insofar as interstate conflicts are concerned, it neverthe -
less will remain sensitive to events happening 
in the Indo-Pacific maritime order. Its posses -
sion of abundant resources and global shipping 
lanes also means it has the potential to stoke 
tensions if this peace does not prevail. 
Washington’s policy prioritization of the Indo- 
Pacific is a pragmatic judgement call, but 
Western governments must not view the 
Indo-Pacific in isolation. The risk is that the 
increasing focus on US-China competition is leading policymakers to adopt a

summary_html:
Main argument: The South Atlantic is a strategically vital but neglected maritime order critical to global trade, resource security, and geopolitical stability. It underpins the security of global supply chains, especially supporting the Indo-Pacific maritime order, and offers alternatives for Western states amid growing great power rivalry, notably between the US and China.

Research design: The article undertakes a qualitative strategic analysis rooted in contemporary maritime order theory and grand strategy debates, supplemented by regional case studies and policy reviews to assess the South Atlantic’s geoeconomic and geopolitical significance.

Method: The method involves conceptual synthesis of maritime order literature combined with documentary analysis of government strategies, policy statements, and secondary sources. It also incorporates geopolitical assessment of regional resources, infrastructure, and great power presence.

Dataset or evidence: Evidence includes official strategic documents from Western and regional states, trade volume data on shipping routes, resource production statistics, and analyses of regional multilateral initiatives such as ZOPACAS, alongside scholarly and policy literature on maritime security and geoeconomics.

Unit of analysis: The primary unit is the South Atlantic maritime order, defined as the expansive maritime region between South America and Africa below the equator, including its states, shipping lanes, and related geostrategic infrastructure.

Time period studied: The study focuses mainly on developments from the post-Cold War era to early 2020s, with attention to evolving great power competition dynamics up to 2025.

Geographic focus: The South Atlantic Ocean region between Africa and South America below the equator, covering roughly 80 countries predominantly in the Global South, including key states like Brazil, Argentina, Nigeria, and South Africa.

Identification strategy: The article identifies the South Atlantic’s strategic value through cross-comparative analysis of maritime order significance, tracing evidence of increasing trade volumes through its sea lanes, regional resource wealth, gaps in Western grand strategy, and emerging contestation by China and Russia.

Key findings: 1) The South Atlantic is fundamental to global maritime trade, resource security, and supply chain resilience, especially as alternative routes amid contested Indo-Pacific order. 2) Western neglect of the region risks ceding influence to adversaries like China and Russia. 3) Indigenous multilateral frameworks such as ZOPACAS offer a viable path for fostering regional security and governance. 4) Western engagement should prioritize inclusive, multilateral cooperation and soft power over militarization to maintain stability and legitimacy.

Main limitations: The article mainly relies on qualitative and policy analysis without primary empirical data collection or quantitative modeling. Its assessment of internal regional political dynamics and geopolitical rivalries may underplay complex local factors. The unpredictability of future great power policies, especially under differing US administrations, poses uncertainty.

Why this matters for IR scholars: This study challenges dominant IR focus on the Indo-Pacific by highlighting the interdependence of maritime orders in the global system and the strategic importance of neglected regions. It urges scholars to reconsider grand strategy frameworks by integrating overlooked spaces, thereby enriching understanding of maritime geoeconomics, multipolarity, and regional governance norms.

Why this matters for strategic infrastructure research: The findings reveal the South Atlantic as a critical node in global supply chain infrastructure, including key chokepoints like Cape Horn and the Panama Canal alternatives, and as a resource-rich maritime order bracing industrial and technological competition. Recognizing this region’s role is essential for designing resilient energy and mineral supply chains, AI governance reliant on critical minerals, and sustainable industrial policies amid growing great power competition.

title: The Gulf's evolving security mosaic: balancing the manifest retrenchment and latent influence of the United States
abstract: Abstract The Gulf region's security architecture appears to be undergoing a fundamental transformation. US military forces are gradually withdrawing, Gulf states are asserting unprecedented autonomy and competing powers are expanding their regional influence. Yet these visible shifts mask deeper continuities. This article examines this apparent paradox through a novel interdisciplinary framework that distinguishes between manifest indicators of change and latent mechanisms of persistent influence. While conventional analyses focus on visible metrics—military deployments, diplomatic realignments and formal agreements—this study reveals how technological dependencies, infrastructural networks and knowledge regimes perpetuate American influence despite apparent withdrawal. The analysis reveals three critical mechanisms sustaining US influence: ‘digital lock-in’ through software-dependent weapons systems, creating ‘weaponized interdependence’; persistent physical infrastructure networks providing operational access and surge capacity; and human capital development that embeds dominant western security paradigms. These mechanisms highlight the temporal asymmetry between rapidly shifting political alignments and the slower evolution of technological dependencies. Rather than witnessing a dramatic restructuring, the Gulf exhibits ‘residual hegemony’, where diminishing material presence coexists with enduring normative, technical and institutional legacies. This reconceptualization offers a more nuanced theoretical understanding of how regional security architectures evolve, suggesting that the most durable forms of influence may reside in socio-technical systems rather than in formal security arrangements. For policy-makers, this indicates that sustainable engagement increasingly depends on technical embeddedness rather than conventional military presence or diplomatic pronouncements.

The security architecture of the Gulf region appears to be at a critical inflec-
tion point.1  The long-established Pax Americana, which has dominated regional 
security dynamics for decades, shows signs of transformation across multiple 
dimensions.2  This shift manifests most visibly in the gradual drawdown of 
American military force posture, with successive administrations since Barack 
Obama demonstrating increasing reluctance to maintain and expand the US’ 
regional footprint.3  Concurrent with this apparent US retrenchment, other global 
powers—including China, the United Kingdom and Turkey—have steadily 
expanded their strategic presence through enhanced arms sales, bilateral military 
relationships, trade agreements and the establishment of military facilities in 
and around the region. 4  Simultaneously, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) 
states have displayed unprecedented willingness and capability to assert their own 
security interests and project power both regionally and internationally, marking 
a stark departure from their historical reliance on US security guarantees. 5

While these developments suggest a transformation in regional order, the 
prevailing discourse frequently oversimplifies complex realities. This study 
addresses this analytical gap through a rigorous examination of contemporary 
geopolitical security engagement across the Gulf, employing a dual analytical 
framework that examines both manifest and latent aspects of regional security 
dynamics—a methodological approach that is well established in social sciences—
to critically assess whether Pax Americana’s widely presumed decline withstands 
scrutiny. While the manifest changes in the Gulf ’s security landscape are indeed 
striking and contribute to a narrative of diminishing US engagement, this study’s 
distinctive contribution lies in its examination of the less visible, liminal elements 
that underpin the continuing Pax Americana. These include US, western and 
NATO-inspired operational norms and doctrinal path dependencies, as well as 
infrastructural arrangements and long-term logistical factors, including a form of 
‘digital lock-in’ to US military materiel which is highly technology-dependent 
and which forms the backbone of most Gulf military forces.
The significance of this inquiry extends beyond academic interest. The region 
remains the epicentre of world energy supply, accounting for 28.8 per cent of 
global crude oil production and 13.1 per cent of natural gas exports through its 
strategic choke points.6  Moreover, with a combined economy of US$1.5 trillion, 
the Gulf states represent a globally significant investment destination whose 
stability has a direct impact on global economic interests.7
The study proceeds by first exploring the origins and application of this analyt-
ical framework, followed by an examination of the Pax Americana’s historical 
evolution to establish a baseline for assessing recent changes. It then analyses 
elements of manifest divergence from the Pax Americana before investigating its 
latent remnants and, finally, concluding.
Latent and manifest elements
This study draws inspiration from a rich intellectual tradition concerned with 
distinguishing between visible phenomena and their less apparent underpin-
nings. Rather than rigidly applying theoretical templates, we embrace concep-
tual insights that illuminate both manifest changes and latent continuities in Gulf 
security architecture. The manifest–latent distinction resonates across diverse 
intellectual traditions. Marx, for example, distinguished between superstructure 
and economic base, Freud between conscious behaviour and unconscious drives 
and Merton between intended and unintended consequences of social actions. 8

These various formulations point toward a fundamental analytical insight: visible 
realities often emerge from and are sustained by less visible forces.
Such concepts may be applied to security studies. Kier examined French 
military doctrine between the world wars, revealing how formal policy positions 
and force structures (manifest elements) emerged from deeply embedded cultural 
assumptions and organizational values (latent factors).9  Kier’s work demonstrated 
not a mechanical application of categories, but an interpretive sensibility attuned 
to multiple dimensions of security dynamics.
In our analysis of Gulf security architecture, manifest dimensions comprise 
identifiable and measurable phenomena: shifts in military force posture (troop 
deployments and base locations), changes in arms sales patterns and formal insti-
tutional arrangements like defence pacts or security cooperation agreements. 10  
These elements can be tracked, quantified and directly observed as the visible 
architecture of regional security relationships.
The latent dimensions comprise underlying, liminal or veiled forces that simul-
taneously shape security domains’ emergence and persistence. Uncovering these 
elements presents greater methodological challenges than documenting manifest 
factors. Fortunately, scholars across International Relations, sociology and philos-
ophy have developed analytical tools and insights to guide this investigation. Both

A pivotal moment came in 1990–1991 with Operations Desert Shield and 
Desert Storm, under which more than half a million US and allied troops were

deployed across the region. However, Gulf leaders advised against the invasion,

larly after Saudi Arabia’s (and the world’s) largest oil-refining facility was struck 
with unerring accuracy, multiple times, by proxy Iranian missiles and drones in 
September 2019 (see below). 29  Saudi leaders spend hundreds of billions of dollars 
on US equipment, and suffered through decades of deeply difficult relations to 
deter and prevent precisely such an attack, leading many to see this moment as 
an ‘inflection point’ in regional security.30  Moreover, the attacks from Iran and 
Israel on Qatar in June and September 2025 (respectively) further highlighted the 
apparent futility in having for so long invested in the US relationship.31  This, then, 
is the state of Gulf–US relations—decades of deep security cooperation, now 
showing signs of evolution. While analysts point to trends of mutual divergence 
and a diminishing US focus on the Gulf, 32  a careful, holistic analysis of these 
changes and their implications remains to be undertaken.

From the high-water mark of Operations Desert Shield and Storm in 1990–1991, 
when allied troop numbers—predominantly American—reached approxi-
mately  540,000, 33  US regional presence has followed a trajectory of ultimate 
contraction punctuated by episodic surges. While the immediate post-Gulf War 
period saw a reduction in deployed forces, the US simultaneously expanded 
its regional footprint in 1991–1994 through a network of defence cooperation 
agreements with Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), 
complemented by enhanced arrangements with Saudi Arabia and Oman.34  These 
agreements underpinned the establishment on the Arabian Peninsula of some of 
the largest US military installations globally, hosting entire fighter wings and 
brigade-sized armour formations, as well as the United States Fifth Fleet, and 
transforming the Gulf into a cornerstone of American power projection. 35
Significantly, these bases often transcended mere forward operating locations 
to become central nodes in the US global command architecture. The ‘central’ 
segment of the area of responsibility of the United States Central Command 
(CENTCOM)—which spanned from the coast of north-east Africa to central 
and south Asia—was administered first from a forward headquarters at Prince 
Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and later from Al Udeid in Qatar, underscoring 
the Gulf ’s pivotal role in American strategic calculations.36
The fluctuations in US troop numbers reflect the Gulf ’s instrumental role in 
supporting operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, rather than a consistent commitment 
to the region per se.37  From approximately 12,000 personnel in the Gulf monar -

in  2011, then steadily declined to approximately 50,000 by  2019 and contracted

Competing security actors
There is compelling evidence that the Gulf monarchies are fundamentally trans-
forming their security strategies across three interrelated dimensions: diversifying 
external security partnerships beyond traditional western allies; strengthening 
domestic military capabilities; and demonstrating an unprecedented willing-
ness to project military power independently. This evolution exemplifies what 
Acharya identifies as the reconstitution of regional security dynamics through 
local agency rather than great power dictation, as historical arrangements give way 
to new configurations shaped by indigenous priorities.46
The proliferation of foreign military bases in the Gulf region between  2009 
and 2019 represents a shift in the security architecture that had been dominated 
by US military presence since the British withdrawal ‘east of Suez’ in 1971. 47  This 
new wave of base establishment—including of France’s installation in the UAE 
in 2009, China’s base in Djibouti in 2017 and Turkey’s 2019 Qatar facility, as well 
as the UK’s ‘permanent’ return in 2018 to Bahrain and Oman—reflects both the 
growing strategic importance of the Gulf and the increasingly multipolar nature 
of global power projection. 48  Through the lens of Merton’s functional analysis, 
these bases serve manifest functions of power projection for establishing nations, 
but also serve latent functions in providing Gulf states with leverage in their rela-
tionships with the US.49

have expanded their provision of training, advisory support, joint exercises 
and defence-industrial cooperation across the Gulf. Turkey has increasingly

provider of training, 50  while China hosts growing numbers of Gulf military 
officers for professional military education courses, technical training and

Growing Gulf autonomy
While Gulf monarchies have spent more than US$1.5 trillion on their military 
forces,59  in the twentieth century and the first decade of the 2000s, the simple 
reality was that these forces were seldom used kinetically and were almost never 
deployed offensively abroad as a tool of state policy. This began to change from 
the Arab Spring onwards. The first contemporary venture of this ilk occurred 
when, to the surprise of most commentators, Qatar and the UAE deployed their 
air forces in multilateral operations against in Libya in 2011. 60
Unexpected as this was, a more significant manifestation of Gulf military 
adventurism and partial autonomy emerged in 2015 when Saudi Arabia assembled 
the largest military coalition in Arab history—named Desert Sword, in a deliberate 
echo of the US-led Desert Shield and Desert Storm operations of 1990–1991—to 
attack Houthi forces in Yemen that threatened Saudi interests and territory.61  For 
Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, the Houthi threat was deemed existential, with Houthi 
forces occupying southern Saudi towns and launching missiles deep into Gulf 
territories. This campaign marked an unprecedented development: never in their 
contemporary histories had the Gulf monarchies deployed military forces in such 
a kinetic, operational manner. Operations such as the UAE’s amphibious landing 
near Aden in 2015—the largest of its type in contemporary Arab history—demon-
strated new capabilities and a willingness to use military power independently.62
While these operations remain unprecedented and, as such, represent an impor-
tant moment in contemporary Gulf military operational history, US support 
remained critical. Interestingly, Gulf leaders assumed that the US would whole-
heartedly support these operations, such was the extent of US–Gulf military 
engagement over preceding decades. However, this was not the case, as the US did 
not provide front-line support. Nevertheless, American support remained vital, 
including logistical support, air-to-air refuelling and intelligence-sharing.63

summary_html:
Main argument: The Gulf security architecture is undergoing a complex transformation characterized by a visible US military retrenchment alongside persistent, underlying American influence embedded in regional military systems, doctrines, and infrastructural dependencies. The Gulf monarchies are diversifying their security partnerships and asserting greater autonomy, but latent elements of the Pax Americana continue to shape regional security dynamics.

Research design: The study employs a dual analytical framework distinguishing manifest (visible) and latent (hidden) elements of Gulf security to critically assess the validity of claims about the decline of US influence and the evolution of regional order.

Method: Qualitative analysis based on historical tracing, doctrinal examination, and institutional theory drawing from IR, sociology, and philosophy literatures. It analyzes military deployments, base infrastructure, arms sales, institutional norms, and strategic behaviors to understand regional security shifts.

Dataset or evidence: Secondary data including official US defense reports on troop deployments and basing, arms sales records, public statements, academic and policy literature, contemporaneous news reports, and historical case studies of Gulf-US relations and emerging regional security actors such as China and Turkey.

Unit of analysis: Security architecture of the Gulf region, focusing on US military presence, Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states’ military capabilities, and external actors’ (China, UK, Turkey) growing roles within Gulf military and political security frameworks.

Time period studied: Primarily post-World War II developments with a focus on the period from the 1990 Gulf War through to 2025, emphasizing events such as US troop surges and drawdowns, the 2019 Saudi oil facility attacks, and recent Gulf military exercises and partnerships.

Geographic focus: The Gulf region, specifically the member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council and adjacent strategic areas involving US and competing great power military activities.

Identification strategy: Triangulation of manifest visible metrics (troop numbers, base locations, arms sales) with latent institutional and doctrinal indicators (norms, operational practices, infrastructural dependencies) to reveal continuities despite apparent shifts in formal US engagement in the Gulf.

Key findings: US military presence in the Gulf has visibly contracted over the past three decades, highlighting a shift toward a more multipolar security landscape with rising roles of China, Turkey, and the UK. Gulf states are increasingly capable and willing to project military power independently and diversify alliances. However, latent dependencies like entrenched US military materiel systems, operational doctrines, and institutional socialization sustain American influence beneath the surface. The 2019 missile and drone attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure marked a critical inflection point exposing limits of traditional US security guarantees and catalyzing Gulf recalibration toward autonomy and diversified security ties.

Main limitations: Reliance on publicly available secondary sources constrains insight into classified or sensitive strategic deliberations. The study’s interpretive approach to latent dimensions may involve subjective judgments on the degree and nature of US influence, limiting empirical precision. Rapid geopolitical developments post-2025 may alter assessed trends.

Why this matters for IR scholars: This nuanced interrogation of manifest and latent factors challenges simplistic narratives of US decline or Gulf autonomy, offering a more complex understanding of great power competition and alliance dynamics. It highlights institutional and technological continuities that sustain hegemonic influence even amid apparent retrenchment, refining theories of regional order and power projection.

Why this matters for strategic infrastructure research: The study reveals critical insights into the role of technological lock-ins and infrastructural dependencies underpinning US military influence. The Gulf’s energy infrastructure and military systems exemplify how latent technological and operational continuities can sustain strategic power despite visible shifts in deployment. This perspective informs research on the resilience of great power influence shaped through complex infrastructure and technology, vital for understanding industrial policy and geopolitical strategy in contested regions.

title: The ecology of artificial intelligence: energy, water, materials, and land limits of digital systems
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is promoted as a tool for ecological sustainability, yet the ecological effects of AI itself remain poorly understood. Existing studies document aspects of AI’s footprint, including energy demand, water withdrawals, mineral extraction, and land occupation, but treat these impacts in isolation. This article develops an integrated resource nexus framework that situates AI within global environmental systems’ energy–water–material–land metabolism. Drawing on recent evidence, we synthesize quantitative estimates of AI’s resource intensity, from thousands of megawatt-hours and millions of liters required to train frontier models, to embodied mineral and land footprints embedded in semiconductor production and hyperscale data centers. We show that these demands are systemic, entangled, and spatially uneven, with benefits concentrated in the Global North and ecological costs externalized to resource frontiers in the Global South. The contribution of this article is twofold. First, it presents a novel conceptual model of AI as a socio-metabolic infrastructure, highlighting the entropic trade-offs associated with digital expansion. Second, it derives governance pathways, including AI-specific environmental impact assessments, multi-dimensional ecological metrics, and spatially responsible siting strategies that embed AI within planetary boundary frameworks. By reframing AI as an ecological actor with biophysical limits, we advance environmental systems research beyond narrow carbon accounting toward a holistic understanding of digital infrastructures in the Anthropocene.

The ecology of artificial intelligence: energy,

systems
Sibongiseni Hlabisa1* 
Abstract 
Artificial intelligence (AI) is promoted as a tool for ecological sustainability, yet the ecological effects of AI itself remain 
poorly understood. Existing studies document aspects of AI’s footprint, including energy demand, water withdraw-
als, mineral extraction, and land occupation, but treat these impacts in isolation. This article develops an integrated 
resource nexus framework that situates AI within global environmental systems’ energy–water–material–land metab-
olism. Drawing on recent evidence, we synthesize quantitative estimates of AI’s resource intensity, from thousands 
of megawatt-hours and millions of liters required to train frontier models, to embodied mineral and land footprints 
embedded in semiconductor production and hyperscale data centers. We show that these demands are systemic, 
entangled, and spatially uneven, with benefits concentrated in the Global North and ecological costs externalized 
to resource frontiers in the Global South. The contribution of this article is twofold. First, it presents a novel conceptual 
model of AI as a socio-metabolic infrastructure, highlighting the entropic trade-offs associated with digital expansion. 
Second, it derives governance pathways, including AI-specific environmental impact assessments, multi-dimensional 
ecological metrics, and spatially responsible siting strategies that embed AI within planetary boundary frameworks. By 
reframing AI as an ecological actor with biophysical limits, we advance environmental systems research beyond nar-
row carbon accounting toward a holistic understanding of digital infrastructures in the Anthropocene.
Keywords Artificial Intelligence, Ecological effects, Energy–water–material–land Nexus, Digital infrastructures, 
Environmental governance, Planetary boundaries
1 Introduction
Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a defining feature 
of contemporary technological and environmental tran -
sitions. From climate modeling and biodiversity moni -
toring to energy optimization, AI is often portrayed as 
a cornerstone of sustainability innovation (Kaack et  al. 
2022; Lhoumeau, et al. 2025; Rolnick et al. 2022). How -
ever, beneath its digital abstraction lies a rapidly expand -
ing physical infrastructure whose ecological footprint 
remains poorly understood.
Data centers, high-performance computing clusters, 
and semiconductor fabrication plants (fabs) consume 
substantial amounts of energy, water, materials, and 
land. These systems translate informational processing 
into material throughput, linking the digital economy to 
global patterns of extraction, pollution, and habitat loss. 
As Mytton (2021) and Ruberti (2024) show, the expan -
sion of AI infrastructure has intensified local conflicts 
over electricity supply, water allocation, and land occupa-
tion, particularly in ecologically sensitive or water-scarce 
regions such as Arizona, Singapore, and Taiwan.
Despite the growing number of reports on AI’s 
energy demand, few studies integrate its multi-resource 
metabolism, which encompasses the combined use of 
energy, water, materials, and land required to sustain its

computational operations. The absence of such integra -
tion hinders our ability to evaluate AI’s actual ecological 
trade-offs and systemic vulnerabilities.
This article addresses this gap by situating AI within the 
resource nexus framework, which conceptualizes envi -
ronmental pressures as interdependent rather than iso -
lated. It adopts a socio-metabolic approach, combining 
quantitative synthesis and conceptual systems analysis 
to trace how digital infrastructures transform and appro -
priate biophysical resources. The analysis examines how 
much energy AI consumes, how water and land avail -
ability shape its spatial distribution, how material supply 
chains underpin its hardware production, and how these 
resource flows interact as an integrated system. It also 
examines the implications of these interconnections for 
environmental governance and the pursuit of sustainable 
digital transitions.
By integrating quantitative estimates with conceptual 
insights, this article provides one of the first comparative 
assessments of AI’s ecological metabolism. Its broader 
aim is to clarify how the infrastructures enabling artifi -
cial intelligence both depend on and reshape the Earth’s 
material foundations, and what this means for governing 
the digital age within planetary boundaries.
2  Methods
This study combines systematic literature synthesis with 
a socio-metabolic conceptual framework to examine the 
ecological dimensions of artificial intelligence. Rather 
than treating energy, water, materials, and land as sepa -
rate categories of impact, the analysis approaches them 
as components of an interdependent system: a resource 
nexus through which AI’s environmental footprint can be 
more accurately understood.
A systematic search was conducted across Web of Sci -
ence, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases to identify 
studies published between 2015 and 2025 that quantified 
or analyzed AI-related environmental impacts. Search 
terms included combinations such as “artificial intel-
ligence” AND “energy consumption”, “data center water 
use”, “semiconductor fabrication environment”, and “data 
infrastructure land use”.
After the initial search returned approximately 
3,130,000 records, automated and manual screening were 
conducted in several stages. First, database filters were 
applied to restrict the search to English-language pub -
lications, peer-reviewed journals, and the period from 
2015 to 2025, reducing the pool to approximately 18,300 
studies. Second, keyword refinement was used to retain 
only studies explicitly addressing environmental aspects 
of artificial intelligence, such as “energy use, ” “water foot-
print, ” “materials, ” “data centers, ” or “semiconductor fabri-
cation”, further narrowing the sample to 312 records.
A title and abstract screening then excluded conceptual 
or social science papers that lacked empirical environ -
mental data. The remaining 94 papers were assessed in 
full text, of which 56 met all inclusion criteria, namely: 
quantitative or model-based resource estimates, rele -
vance to core AI infrastructures, and adequate methodo -
logical transparency for comparison.
After successive screening and eligibility checks, 46 
sources were retained for analysis (see Fig.  1). The final 
corpus comprises 22 peer-reviewed publications (journal 
articles and refereed proceedings), 17 technical, policy, 
or industry reports (including government and corporate 
sustainability documents), four preprints/white papers, 
and three scholarly books or encyclopedia chapters. 
This mix balances empirical rigour and up-to-date tech -
nical insight, spanning foundational socio-metabolic 
and planetary boundaries research, quantitative stud -
ies of data centre energy and water use, and semicon -
ductor manufacturing impacts. Together, these sources 
span the interdisciplinary landscape of environmental 
systems research, ranging from socio-metabolic theory 
(Fischer-Kowalski & Haberl 2007; Krausmann et al. 2008) 
and planetary boundaries (Rockström et  al. 2009; Stef -
fen et al. 2015) to contemporary analyses of data center 
energy and water consumption (LBNL 2024; Li et  al. 
2023; Mytton 2021) and semiconductor manufacturing 
impacts (Ruberti 2023, 2024).
The selected literature was analyzed through a qualita -
tive–quantitative synthesis, extracting key metrics such 
as electricity demand per model training run, water with-
drawal per megawatt-hour, embodied emissions per sem-
iconductor unit, and average land footprint of hyperscale 
data centers and fabrication plants. Reported values were 
normalized to a common unit to facilitate cross-domain 
comparison.
Where possible, values were aggregated into repre -
sentative ranges (e.g., 1.3–1.5 GWh per training run; 
7,000–12,000 L per MWh for data center cooling) and 
cross-checked against recent environmental assessments 
(LBNL 2024; Mytton 2021; Ruberti 2023). These data 
were then contextualized through socio-metabolic rea -
soning, emphasizing how resource inputs and waste out -
puts circulate through AI’s infrastructural systems.
2.1  Conceptual framework: the socio‑metabolic nexus 
of AI
The analytical framework builds on the socio-metabolic 
theory of environmental systems (Fischer-Kowalski & 
Haberl 2007; Krausmann et  al. 2008), which conceptu -
alizes societies as energy–material systems sustained 
through continuous exchanges with the biosphere. This 
is integrated with the planetary boundaries framework 
(Rockström et  al. 2009) to contextualize these flows

Hlabisa  Carbon Neutral Systems            (2025) 1:19 
 
within Earth’s safe operating space. Together, they offer 
a biophysical lens for analyzing AI’s environmental rela -
tions. This framework highlights how computational 
infrastructures depend on the extraction, transformation, 
and spatial concentration of biophysical resources.
As illustrated in Fig. 2, AI functions as a metabolic sub-
system that converts information into control capacity, 
sustained by flows of energy, water, and materials, and 
embedded within land-based infrastructure. The diagram 
captures both resource inputs (electricity, minerals, puri -
fied water) and entropic outputs (waste heat, pollution, 
and ecological displacement). This framing enables the 
analysis of AI as a technological and thermodynamically 
open subsystem of the global economy.
2.2  Limitations
While systematic in approach, this review is constrained 
by the scarcity and variability of available data. Many 
environmental estimates rely on modeled or proprietary 
values rather than empirical reporting, and few sources 
disaggregate AI-specific resource use from broader ICT 
infrastructure. Quantitative synthesis therefore, empha -
sizes representative orders of magnitude rather than pre -
cise totals. Despite these limitations, the integration of 
multiple data types and sources enables a coherent view 
of AI’s emergent ecological profile and highlights critical 
areas for future empirical research.
3  Results: the resource nexus of AI
The synthesis of 46 selected sources reveals that artificial 
intelligence infrastructures exhibit substantial and inter -
linked demands for energy, water, materials, and land. 
These dependencies are mutually reinforcing, forming 
a socio-ecological metabolism in which each resource 
dimension intensifies the others. The findings are organ -
ized below around these four domains and their cross-
domain interactions.
3.1  Overview of resource intensities
Across all studies, AI’s ecological metabolism emerges 
as a resource-dense and spatially concentrated phenom -
enon. As shown in Table  1, training a single large model, 
such as GPT-3 or PaLM-2, can consume between 1.3 and 
1.5 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of electricity, roughly equiva -
lent to the annual energy usage of a small town (Patterson 
et al. 2021). At the global scale, total AI-related electricity 
demand could reach 150–300 TWh yr⁻ 1 by 2028, a three- 
to five-fold increase from 2022 (LBNL 2024).
Water withdrawals show a comparable magnitude. 
Data-center cooling typically requires 7,000–12,000 L

3.3  Water
Water plays a dual role in AI infrastructure, serving as 
both a cooling agent and an enabler of precision manu -
facturing. In data centers, water usage is influenced by 
the local climate and cooling design, with evaporative 
systems typically prevailing in arid regions. In semicon -

multiplies the embodied energy of each wafer, creating 
a hidden hydrological burden. In areas such as Arizona, 
Singapore, and Taiwan, competition among industrial, 
municipal, and agricultural users has already led to epi -

2021; Narvaez 2022). From a socio-metabolic perspec -
tive, water functions as a thermodynamic sink, allowing 
the dissipation of computational heat and linking digital 
performance directly to ecological stress.

gains. The “Rapid AI Adoption” scenario illustrates a con-

Material use anchors AI’s dependence on extractive 
industries. Advanced processors and memory chips

Their extraction generates extensive ecological exter -

ments in eco-efficiency, the environmental intensity of 
chip production has plateaued because each generation 
demands cleaner rooms and greater throughput. This 
pattern illustrates an entropic escalation: maintaining a 
higher informational order requires a disproportionate 
amount of material and energetic input, deepening AI’s 
entanglement with global supply chains and contributing 
to environmental degradation.
Figures  6 and 7 provide a visual illustration of 
the “entropic escalation” inherent in AI’s physical 
infrastructure.
Figure  6  quantifies the central paradox outlined by 
Ruberti (2023, 2024): despite incremental improvements 
in eco-efficiency, the resource intensity of chip manufac -
turing surges with each new generation. The left panel 
clearly shows this divergence, as the industry progresses 
from 28 to 2 nm nodes, eco-efficiency plateaus, while the 
demand for resources skyrockets. This occurs because 
the gains from technical efficiency are overwhelmed by 
the escalating costs of purity and precision, such as the 
need for vast clean rooms and ultra-pure materials. The 
right panel further contextualizes this issue, revealing 
that AI-optimized chips are not marginally, but substan -
tially, more resource-hungry, demanding up to 4.5 times 
more water and rare earth elements than traditional 
chips. This chart captures the essence of entropic esca -
lation: achieving a higher state of informational order 
(more powerful AI) requires a disproportionately larger 
input of material and energy.
Figure 7 expands this linear progression into a systemic 
model, illustrating how the environmental impacts of AI 
hardware form a self-reinforcing cycle. The circular flow 
demonstrates that the consequences are not confined to a 
single stage but are interconnected. For instance, the haz-
ardous e-waste resulting from disposal (a consequence 
of the complex chips shown in Fig.  6) can lead to soil 
and water contamination, which in turn exacerbates the 
ecological damage and resource scarcity associated with 
the initial extraction phase. This creates a feedback loop

by the consequences of another. The diagram thus moves 
beyond a simple supply chain to show why the environ -
mental challenge is so persistent and difficult to solve; the

own resource demands and ecological footprint.
3.5  Land and space
AI’s land footprint reflects the physical manifestation of 
its infrastructure, a transformation vividly captured in 
the accompanying figures. Figure 8 provides a stark visual 
testimony to this phenomenon, mapping how clusters of 
data centers and fabs transform peri-urban and agricul -
tural landscapes into specialized industrial zones. The 
land-use charts quantify this shift, showing how regions 
like Ireland and Singapore have seen AI infrastructure 
claim a significant portion of their land, directly displac -
ing agricultural and other uses. This global snapshot con-
textualizes the specific policy responses you cite; the map 
clearly shows Ireland and Singapore categorized under 
‘Moratorium’ and ‘Conditional’ status, a direct result of 
them hitting the capacity limits acknowledged in their 
government statements.
The long-term implications of this spatial transforma -
tion are explored in  Fig.  9. It powerfully illustrates the 
concept of path dependency, demonstrating how large 
semiconductor clusters, such as Hsinchu Science Park 
and Arizona’s corridor, lock land into industrial func -
tion for decades. The infrastructure life-cycle chart 
illustrates a multi-decade “lock-in” period, resulting 
in the very spatial inflexibility that constrains alterna -
tive ecological or social uses. Furthermore, the trade-off  
analysis explains  why this inflexibility is so critical: while 
AI infrastructure scores high on economic capacity, 
it scores lowest on ecological value and flexibility, the 
very qualities needed for sustainable and adaptive land 
management.
Finally,  Fig. 10  offers a systemic diagnosis of the lim -
its being reached. Its multi-dimensional analysis shows 
that the moratorium in Ireland and the conditional lift 
in Singapore were not arbitrary but were triggered by a 
convergence of critical constraints. These regions, along 
with other hotspots such as Virginia, are shown pushing 
against red-line thresholds not just in land allocation, but 
also in grid capacity, water stress, and regulatory pres -
sure simultaneously. This figure moves beyond anecdo -
tal evidence to provide an integrated model that explains 
why the reconfiguration of regional land use creates such 
complex and binding constraints on future development.
3.6  Nexus interactions
The four resource domains interact in non-linear ways. 
Higher energy use increases cooling demand, which in 
turn leads to increased water withdrawals. Water scarcity 
can restrict energy production and chip fabrication, both 
of which depend on material extraction that transforms 
landscapes. These feedbacks form a coupled resource-
nexus system, in which local efficiency gains may pro -
duce global environmental costs.
Understanding AI’s ecological footprint, therefore, 
requires moving beyond single-metric accounting toward 
an integrated, systemic analysis. The nexus perspective 
highlights that the combined pressures of energy avail -
ability, water scarcity, material throughput, and land use 
constrain the growth of AI. These interactions set the 
stage for the discussion that follows, which interprets the

4  Discussion
The synthesis of forty-six sources reveals that the envi -
ronmental footprint of artificial intelligence (AI) extends 
well beyond electricity consumption. AI operates 
through a multi-resource metabolism in which energy, 
water, materials, and land are tightly coupled. This inter -
dependence produces both efficiency gains and systemic 
vulnerabilities. Despite rapid technical improvements, 
the broader pattern suggests a deepening resource 
dependence that scales faster than gains in efficiency or 
substitution can offset.
4.1  Complexity, efficiency, and the paradox of control
A recurring pattern across the reviewed literature is 
the contradiction between technological efficiency and 
aggregate environmental load, a dynamic often captured 
by the Jevons paradox (Sorrell 2009). As AI architectures

hardware systems. Each stage feeds back into environmental degradation, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of resource intensity

evolve, each generation of hardware and software 
becomes markedly more efficient at processing informa -
tion. Google’s 2024 Environmental Sustainability Report, 
for example, documents more than a 30-fold reduction 
in energy required per inference within just a single year 
of optimization. Similar trends are visible in NVIDIA’s 
shift from the A100 to the H100 architecture, where per -
formance per watt has increased dramatically (NVIDIA 
2022a; 2022b). Yet, as these improvements lower the 
marginal cost of computation, they stimulate broader 
deployment of AI services, expanding both total compu -
tational throughput and the physical infrastructure that 
supports it.
This feedback produces what might be called an effi -
ciency–complexity spiral. Each incremental improve -
ment in efficiency enables the design of larger models,

and residential land to industrial AI clusters

high economic value but low ecological and flexibility scores

denser data centres, and more pervasive applications. 
In doing so, efficiency gains are quickly reinvested into 
greater system complexity. Empirical evidence from the 
data-center sector confirms this pattern: although the 
average energy use per computation has fallen, global 
electricity consumption by data centers continues to 
grow at roughly 15–20 percent annually (LBNL 2024). 
Water consumption follows a similar trajectory, as cool -
ing demand scales with total thermal output, even as 
individual servers become more efficient (Mytton 2021). 
The apparent decoupling of performance from environ -
mental cost thus proves temporary; aggregate demand 
outpaces efficiency.
From a thermodynamic perspective, this outcome 
reflects a fundamental constraint of open systems. Main -
taining and expanding informational order requires a 
continuous inflow of energy and matter, along with an 
outflow of waste heat and entropy. The more intricate 
the informational structure, be it a neural network or a 
planetary economy, the greater the energetic throughput 
required to sustain it. In this sense, the pursuit of con -
trol through computation inevitably deepens material 
dependence. The growth of AI, therefore, parallels the 
broader pattern of industrial civilization described in 
socio-metabolic theory (Fischer-Kowalski & Haberl 2007; 
Krausmann et  al. 2008): progress in informational com -
plexity drives expansion in biophysical metabolism.
The paradox of control lies in the fact that systems 
seeking greater control over their environment must 
expend increasing amounts of energy to maintain that 
very control (Hlabisa 2025). In AI, this is manifested in 
escalating requirements for data storage, redundancy, 
cybersecurity, and algorithmic refinement, all of which 
consume additional computational cycles and hence 
additional energy. The outcome is a self-reinforcing loop: 
the more AI is used to optimize energy systems, logis -
tics, or agriculture, the more computational infrastruc -
ture is required to support these optimizations. What 
emerges is not a linear path toward dematerialization,
