and regulatory frameworks across regions
Page 12 of 20Hlabisa  Carbon Neutral Systems            (2025) 1:19 
but a circular process in which efficiency generates new 
domains of dependency.
This insight challenges prevailing narratives of “green 
AI, ” which often assume that algorithmic optimization 
will automatically yield sustainability benefits. While 
local efficiencies are real and sometimes substantial, they 
are embedded within a global system whose total ener -
getic and material demands are rising. The policy impli -
cation is that sustainability cannot be achieved solely 
through efficiency improvements; it requires explicit 
constraints on total computational growth and a shift 
from efficiency-based metrics to sufficiency-based gov -
ernance. Without such systemic limits, the energetic 
metabolism of AI will continue to accelerate even as indi-
vidual devices become cleaner or faster.
4.2  Spatial concentration and systems vulnerability
The global infrastructure sustaining artificial intelligence 
is characterized by extraordinary spatial concentration. 
Production, computation, and storage are concentrated 
within a limited number of industrial and climatic nodes, 
notably Taiwan, the United States, Ireland, and Singa -
pore, each of which hosts large-scale semiconductor 
fabrication plants or hyperscale data centres. This pat -
tern mirrors broader trends in socio-metabolic systems, 
where technological specialization yields efficiency at the 
cost of geographical resilience. As Monstadt and Saltz -
man (2025) observe, the “digital gateways” of Europe are 
physically materialized in a handful of infrastructural 
corridors, which concentrate energy flows, land conver -
sion, and risk exposure.
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company 
(TSMC) offers a striking example. Its operations in Hsin -
chu Science Park alone account for billions of liters of 
annual freshwater use, extensive electricity demand, and 
significant waste heat emissions (TSMC 2022; Ruberti 
2024). During the 2021 drought, water shortages com -
pelled authorities to reallocate supplies from agriculture 
to semiconductor production (Narvaez 2022), dem -
onstrating how AI’s physical backbone directly com -
petes with food systems and rural livelihoods. A similar 
dynamic is emerging in Arizona’s semiconductor cor -
ridor, where water withdrawals for new fabs are pro -
voking public concern (Lepawsky 2024). These cases 
highlight how digital infrastructures are not only depend-
ent on natural resources but also actively reshape their 
allocation.
In Europe, and particularly in Ireland, the concentra -
tion of data centers has led to tensions between industrial 
growth and public sustainability goals. The Government 
of Ireland’s (2022) statement on data centers explic -
itly acknowledges that energy grid constraints and 
water availability limit further expansion, resulting in a 
temporary moratorium on new developments. Singapore 
has adopted comparable measures, imposing a construc -
tion freeze in 2019 and subsequently allowing only con -
ditional approvals tied to efficiency and heat-recovery 
performance (DataCenter Dynamics 2022). Together, 
these examples illustrate how spatial saturation and 
resource competition are emerging as critical governance 
frontiers for digital economies.
Spatial concentration also amplifies systemic vulnera -
bility. In resilience theory, systems that centralize critical 
functions in a few nodes exhibit high efficiency but low 
redundancy (Pisano 2012). In the AI sector, concentra -
tion magnifies exposure to environmental hazards, sup -
ply chain disruptions, and geopolitical shocks. A drought 
in Taiwan, a heatwave in Ireland, or an energy crisis in 
Europe can have a ripple effect across global information 
flows, potentially disrupting AI model training, cloud 
services, and dependent sectors such as finance, logistics, 
or environmental monitoring. From a socio-metabolic 
perspective, this pattern resembles entropy localization, 
where the accumulation of environmental and thermody-
namic stress occurs in a few sites, allowing informational 
order to be maintained elsewhere.
The geographic asymmetry of this system reflects 
the externalization logic of global production. High-
value informational outputs are generated in the global 
North, while many of the ecological and material costs 
are absorbed by resource-intensive industrial nodes in 
Asia and the Middle East (Ali et  al. 2017; UNEP 2020). 
This asymmetry reproduces older patterns of envi -
ronmental inequality under a new digital guise. While 
AI applications are often promoted as tools for global 
optimization (enhancing crop yields, monitoring bio -
diversity, or improving logistics), their infrastructural 
underpinnings remain materially and spatially exclusion -
ary, requiring secure energy and water access that many 
regions cannot afford.
This concentration further undermines systemic resil -
ience. The principle of redundancy, which involves main-
taining multiple, geographically distributed systems to 
buffer against local shocks, is largely absent in AI infra -
structure design. Instead, hyperscale data centers and 
fabrication clusters seek economies of scale through 
aggregation, producing single points of environmental 
and geopolitical failure. As LBNL (2024) and Shehabi 
et al. (2024) note, the majority of global data processing 
is now handled by fewer than one hundred sites, each 
consuming gigawatt-scale power. The vulnerability of 
such a system lies in its environmental exposure and its 
dependence on continuous flows of energy, materials, 
and cooling resources, which climate change and political 
instability increasingly threaten.

Hlabisa  Carbon Neutral Systems            (2025) 1:19 
 
A broader implication is that digital concentration is 
becoming a new form of ecological risk. Just as global 
agriculture has become vulnerable through monocul -
tures, the digital economy’s concentration in a few indus-
trial ecologies introduces fragility on a planetary scale. 
This suggests a need to rethink spatial governance for AI 
infrastructure, including decentralizing data processing, 
diversifying geographic locations, and integrating local 
renewable energy and water resources. Policies that man-
date environmental impact assessments, resilience plan -
ning, and equitable resource allocation can help prevent 
AI’s material concentration from translating into sys -
temic collapse.
From the standpoint of socio-metabolic theory, the 
pattern is unmistakable: AI’s expansion reproduces the 
metabolic geography of industrial modernity, in which 
the control of information depends on the extraction and 
concentration of energy and matter in limited spaces. The 
apparent intangibility of artificial intelligence thus rests 
on intensely territorial and ecological foundations.
4.3  Biodiversity, land systems, and hidden ecological costs
While the environmental discourse on artificial intel -
ligence (AI) has largely focused on energy consumption 
and carbon emissions, the land-use and biodiversity 
dimensions remain insufficiently recognized. However, as 
the reviewed literature shows, AI’s infrastructure exerts 
growing pressure on terrestrial ecosystems through land 
occupation, habitat fragmentation, and indirect resource-
driven degradation. In effect, the expansion of digital 
infrastructures (data centers, semiconductor foundries, 
transmission corridors, and supporting logistics) repre -
sents a new phase of industrial territorialization, trans -
lating informational growth into physical reconfiguration 
of landscapes (Rosati et  al. 2023; Monstadt & Saltzman 
2025).
Data centers and semiconductor fabrication facilities 
are spatially extensive, often requiring tens to hundreds 
of hectares of serviced land equipped with cooling sys -
tems, substations, and access infrastructure (Roundy 
2025; Ruberti 2024). Once established, these facilities are 
long-lived and spatially inert, remaining operational for 
decades. Their establishment typically entails the per -
manent conversion of agricultural, peri-urban, or semi-
natural landscapes. In Ireland, for instance, community 
opposition to hyperscale data centers has increased in 
response to land-use conflicts and cumulative energy 
demand (Government of Ireland 2022). Similarly, Sin -
gapore’s early moratorium on data center expansion 
reflected concerns about limited land availability and 
ecosystem stress in its already densely populated urban 
environment (DataCenter Dynamics 2022).
This form of land use exemplifies what could be 
described as metabolic enclosure, the appropriation and 
stabilization of land for high-throughput industrial sys -
tems. Once enclosed, such land is effectively withdrawn 
from alternative ecological or social functions. Over 
time, this produces spatial lock-in, whereby environmen -
tal governance becomes constrained by the sunk costs of 
infrastructural investments. Land that might otherwise 
serve as agricultural buffer zones, wetland restoration 
sites, or community commons becomes fixed within a 
high-energy digital economy.
AI’s land footprint is not limited to the built environ -
ment; it extends upstream through resource extrac -
tion and supply chains. Semiconductor manufacturing 
depends on high-purity silicon, copper, cobalt, and rare 
earth elements such as neodymium and terbium (Ali 
et  al. 2017; Wübbeke 2013). The mining and processing 
of these materials often occur in ecologically sensitive 
areas, such as China, Africa, and South America, result -
ing in deforestation, soil contamination, and riverine pol-
lution. For instance, tailings and acid mine drainage from 
rare-earth processing in Inner Mongolia have created 
toxic waste lakes, which have destroyed local vegetation 
and compromised groundwater quality (Wübbeke 2013).
Such upstream degradation represents a hidden land 
cost; a displacement of ecological burden from high-
income, infrastructure-consuming regions to resource-
producing peripheries. This externalization of impact 
reinforces global environmental inequality, whereby 
the biophysical consequences of AI’s growth are dispro -
portionately borne by ecosystems and communities far 
removed from centers of consumption.
Habitat conversion associated with industrial and 
urban expansion remains one of the primary drivers of 
biodiversity decline globally (IPBES 2019). The siting of 
AI infrastructure often coincides with peri-urban biodi -
versity hotspots, due to its proximity to transport corri -
dors and grid infrastructure. Large industrial estates alter 
microclimates, disrupt ecological connectivity, and con -
tribute to urban heat islands, further stressing local flora 
and fauna.
Moreover, the intensification of resource extraction for 
AI hardware compounds this loss. The mining and smelt-
ing of critical minerals involve the destruction of habi -
tats, the introduction of invasive species through road 
networks, and long-term toxic effects on aquatic eco -
systems (Edwards et al. 2014). In biodiversity terms, the 
AI industry therefore acts as both a direct agent of land 
transformation and an indirect amplifier of extractive 
frontiers, accelerating the rate at which natural systems 
are converted into industrial metabolism.
The dematerialized image of digital technology often 
obscures these spatial and ecological impacts. The 
Page 14 of 20Hlabisa  Carbon Neutral Systems            (2025) 1:19 
perception of AI as a low-footprint, knowledge-based 
innovation masks its physical dependence on continu -
ous flows of land, water, and materials. The invisibility 
of these processes within environmental accounting sys -
tems, particularly in nations that host high-end compu -
tational infrastructure, perpetuates a policy blind spot. 
Land-use planning frameworks rarely incorporate digi -
tal infrastructure into biodiversity impact assessments, 
and environmental impact statements typically focus on 
construction-phase emissions rather than operational or 
cumulative ecosystem effects.
From a socio-metabolic perspective, this invisibility is 
symptomatic of an information–material asymmetry: the 
more energy and matter are consumed to sustain digi -
tal order, the more abstracted and immaterial that order 
appears. This paradox of immateriality constitutes a pro -
found challenge for environmental governance. Without 
explicit recognition of AI’s terrestrial footprint, policies 
risk reinforcing the very disconnection between knowl -
edge production and ecological reality that drives unsus -
tainable development.
Recognizing the land dimension of AI’s metabolism 
opens up new pathways for sustainability policy. Incorpo-
rating digital infrastructures into strategic environmental 
assessments, establishing spatial caps on land conversion 
for data and fabrication sites, and developing ecologi -
cal offset mechanisms could help internalize these costs. 
Likewise, adopting biodiversity-sensitive design princi -
ples, such as vegetated cooling systems, landscape buff -
ers, and integration with renewable energy corridors, can 
mitigate local impacts.
However, such measures must be guided by a systemic 
understanding: land conservation cannot be achieved by 
simply relocating environmental burdens elsewhere. As 
Seto et  al. (2012) emphasize, the sustainability of urban 
and industrial systems depends on recognizing land tele -
connections: the distant ecological linkages that connect 
production, consumption, and environmental change 
across scales. In this light, AI’s expansion is not merely 
a technological phenomenon but a spatial and eco -
logical process that demands an integrative governance 
response.
4.4  Water–energy–material nexus: from efficiency 
to sufficiency
A central insight from this review is that the environ -
mental burden of artificial intelligence (AI) cannot be 
understood through any single variable (energy, water, or 
materials) taken in isolation. Instead, these three domains 
interact as a resource nexus that defines the thermody -
namic and ecological metabolism of AI infrastructures. 
Each input reinforces or constrains the others: electricity 
generation depends on water for cooling; semiconductor 
fabrication consumes both energy and ultrapure water; 
and the production of advanced materials requires exten-
sive energy and chemical processing. The overall effect is 
a multiplicative coupling of environmental costs, where 
local improvements in one dimension may worsen pres -
sures in another.
Data centers illustrate this nexus most clearly. As 
computational loads increase, more servers and cooling 
equipment are required, resulting in higher electricity 
and water consumption. Facilities that switch from air to 
evaporative cooling systems to improve energy efficiency 
often increase their water usage (Mytton 2021). Con -
versely, water-free cooling solutions such as closed-loop 
chillers can increase energy demand by 10–15 percent 
(Shehabi et  al. 2024). These trade-offs are context-spe -
cific: in arid regions such as Arizona or the Gulf states, 
electricity generation itself relies on thermoelectric 
plants that withdraw vast volumes of water, compound -
ing local scarcity (Yang & Lant 2011). Thus, reducing one 
environmental metric often amplifies another, creating 
governance dilemmas that are more about substitution 
than resolution.
The semiconductor sector magnifies this coupling. 
A single 300-mm wafer may require up to 2.5  m3 of 
ultrapure water and several hundred kilowatt-hours of 
electricity (Ruberti 2023; TSMC 2022). Purification and 
recirculation systems depend on chemical reagents and 
high-pressure pumps, which themselves consume energy. 
At the same time, the chemicals used in wafer cleaning 
(hydrofluoric acid, hydrogen peroxide, and silicon tet -
rachloride) entail significant embodied emissions and 
toxicity risks (Shen et  al. 2018). The production, trans -
portation, and disposal of these materials form a continu-
ous loop of energy-material exchange that sustains the 
informational order of the digital economy.
Within this coupled nexus, efficiency gains often fail 
to reduce aggregate throughput. Improvements in chip 
architecture or data-center design lower the resource 
cost per computation but stimulate larger computational 
demand. As seen with the transition from NVIDIA’s 
A100 to H100 accelerators, each watt saved per operation 
enables the proliferation of more servers and training 
runs (NVIDIA 2022b; Schneider et  al. 2025). The same 
logic applies to water: reductions in cooling water inten -
sity invite higher server density and greater total heat 
generation. This rebound effect, which illustrates why 
efficiency-enabling growth remains inadequate when 
sustainability strategies focus solely on technological 
optimization (Sorrell 2009), is a key example.
A more robust approach requires shifting the govern -
ing principle from efficiency to sufficiency, the deliberate 
limitation of total resource use within ecological bounda-
ries. In practical terms, this means that efficiency metrics

caps. Data centers, for example, could be licensed based

tas tied to regional hydrological capacity. Semiconductor 
fabs may adopt integrated resource accounting, reporting

summary_html:
Main argument: This study argues that the ecological footprint of artificial intelligence (AI) extends beyond energy consumption to include critical interlinked demands for water, materials, and land, which form a socio-metabolic resource nexus. AI’s growth drives a systemic expansion of physical infrastructure, resulting in entropic trade-offs, spatial concentration, and uneven ecological costs concentrated in the Global South. The paper calls for integrated governance approaches that recognize AI as an ecological actor bounded by planetary limits.

Research design: The article employs a systematic literature review combined with a socio-metabolic conceptual framework. It integrates quantitative synthesis with qualitative systems analysis to map AI’s multi-resource metabolism and assess ecological impacts across interconnected domains of energy, water, materials, and land.

Method: A comprehensive systematic search was conducted across multiple academic and technical databases to identify empirical and model-based evidence on AI’s environmental impacts (2015–2025). Following screening and eligibility criteria, 46 relevant sources were analyzed through qualitative–quantitative synthesis, normalizing and aggregating data to reveal systemic resource use patterns and feedback loops at the intersection of biophysical and technological processes.

Dataset or evidence: The evidence base comprises 22 peer-reviewed publications, 17 technical and policy reports, 4 preprints/white papers, and 3 scholarly books/chapters, collectively covering topics such as data center energy and water use, semiconductor manufacturing impacts, and socio-metabolic environmental theory. Quantitative metrics extracted include electricity use per AI training run, water withdrawal per MWh cooling, embodied emissions of hardware, land footprint of infrastructure, and material intensity of semiconductor production.

Unit of analysis: The primary units of analysis are AI infrastructures: computational hardware (large AI model training, data centers, semiconductor fabrication plants), resource flows (energy, water, materials), and spatial land use patterns related to AI industrial clusters.

Time period studied: The study synthesizes research primarily from 2015 to 2025, with forward-looking projections of AI-related resource demand extending to 2030 and beyond.

Geographic focus: Though global in scope, special focus is given to infrastructure hotspots in the Global North (United States, Europe, Singapore) and resource extraction fronts in the Global South and Asia (Taiwan, China, Africa). Regional case studies highlight areas with significant ecological pressures and governance responses such as Ireland, Arizona, and Hsinchu Science Park.

Identification strategy: The article identifies AI’s ecological footprint by integrating multi-domain quantitative estimates with socio-metabolic theory to surface systemic interactions and spatial concentration effects. It moves beyond single-impact analyses to diagnose feedback loops among energy, water, materials, and land, illustrating how efficiency gains are offset by rebound effects and infrastructure lock-in.

Key findings: - Training large AI models consumes gigawatt-hours of electricity, with global AI demand projected to triple or quintuple by 2028–2030. - Water use for data center cooling and semiconductor fabrication is substantial and growing, especially in water-scarce regions, posing local conflicts. - Material demands for AI hardware, particularly semiconductors, exhibit entropic escalation, with successive generations requiring disproportionately more resources and hazardous inputs. - AI infrastructure occupies extensive land areas, causing habitat loss, spatial lock-in, and socio-ecological displacement, primarily where land is limited. - Resource domains are tightly coupled in a nexus, generating trade-offs and reinforcing systemic vulnerabilities, including spatial concentration in few global hubs. - Efficiency improvements lower marginal costs but stimulate expansion, resulting in a paradoxical rebound effect where aggregate environmental impacts increase. - Governance responses to date include moratoria and conditional permits in regions facing resource constraints, but these must evolve toward integrated, sufficiency-based frameworks that limit total resource use within planetary boundaries.

Main limitations: The study is constrained by variability and gaps in empirical data, especially proprietary or modeled estimates that do not always disaggregate AI-specific resource consumption from broader ICT infrastructure. Quantitative synthesis emphasizes orders of magnitude rather than precise totals and relies on cross-disciplinary sources with differing scopes and methodologies.

Why this matters for IR scholars: This research highlights AI’s geopolitical and environmental externalities embedded in global resource flows and infrastructure concentration, which shape strategic autonomy, industrial policy, and cross-border governance challenges. Understanding AI as a socio-metabolic system reveals state dependencies on critical materials, energy grids, and water supplies concentrated in key regions vulnerable to geopolitical shocks. The findings inform international cooperation on AI governance, technological competition, and sustainable development amidst great power rivalry and resource scarcity.

Why this matters for strategic infrastructure research: By framing AI infrastructure as a strategic socio-metabolic nexus, the paper underscores the intrinsic biophysical constraints on compute power expansion, critical mineral dependencies, and land-use conflicts. This integrated perspective is essential for designing resilient, sustainable AI governance regimes and industrial policies that anticipate systemic vulnerabilities. Policymakers and strategists must consider the environmental limits and spatial lock-ins of AI infrastructure within broader geopolitical and energy security contexts, linking digital technological competition with material resource governance and planetary boundary frameworks.

title: Comments by Mary-Françoise Renard, on  Retaliatory Tariffs of China during the Trade War: A Firm-level Overview
abstract: Mary-Françoise Renard: This paper addresses a significant topic from recent years—the trade war between the United States and China—and specifically examines China's role in imposing retaliatory tariffs on firm imports.The ongoing economic and political tensions between China and the United States significantly shape international relationships. The outcome of this conflict will influence the trajectory of global interactions in the years ahead. Moreover, geopolitics now plays a crucial role in determining economic ties among nations.At the beginning of the 1970s, the United States did not want China to stay out of the global world. Today, they want to push it outside. This is a danger. The United States faces risks, even as the world's leading power, because it remains uncertain how long it can maintain this position. Meanwhile, China actively seeks allies, albeit often for specific issues. The trade war is probably one of the main vectors of this opposition, closely linked to competition over technology, which is the core of the competition between the two countries.Then, the comprehension of these questions is a major issue.The objectives of the paper are to present the results of research on the pass-through of tariffs in the Chinese economy during the trade war with the United States, from the Chinese perspective. These results are compared with those observed in the United States.To study the impact of trade war, the authors have chosen to investigate the pass-through of tariffs to import prices. It allows us to understand the distributional effects. They focus on two points: the exemption of processing imports from retaliatory tariffs in China and the heterogeneous distribution of retaliatory tariffs across product classifications. In the latter case, a distinction is made between products categories, trade regimes, firm ownership structures, and geographical regions. They also give a detailed description of the firm's import tariffs. They remind the reader that approximatively US$ 350 billion of Chinese products had been subjected to tariffs ranging from 10 percent to 50 percent. China imposed six rounds of tariffs on over US$ 100 billion of U.S. products in retaliation.The paper describes the evolution of the trade war and looks at the differences between the sectors. It highlights the fact that the United States wants to hit China's high technology industry while avoiding an increase of consumer goods’ prices. At the same time, China wants to avoid imposing tariffs on intermediate goods imported for the United States because it would be costly for Chinese firms. The two countries have the same strategy, which is to avoid what they consider to be negative outcomes for their domestic market.This resulted in 66 percent of Chinese exports and 58 percent of U.S. exports subject to tariffs in 2020.It is interesting to notice that U.S. tariffs were related to most of intermediate goods imported by the United States and to a lesser extent to some final goods. On the contrary, Chinese retaliatory tariffs were focused on a few sectors—and semiconductors and aircrafts were not subject to tariffs.The objective of the U.S. tariffs is to hit China's high-technology industries.The authors consider that China has been more cautious in its strategy, probably because it is much more engaged in the processing trade. The results are important because they illustrate how trade is a channel for the deterioration of bilateral relationships.The paper's research reveals: A 10 percent increase in China's import duties on products from the United States leads to a 2.75 percent decrease in import value and a 1.51 decrease in import quantity.Firms engaged in more processing activities tend to have lower import tariffs.The average import tariffs do not vary significantly among firms with different ownership.The average import tariffs in the south-eastern regions are relatively lower than in the other regions.Three comments and some suggestions can be made.First, the impact of trade policies has been the subject considerable research, in part because goals are often not achieved and there are many unexpected effects. Then, a historical perspective may be useful, for instance. Alessandria et al. (2022).Second, the regional analysis is an interesting part of the paper, but one point should be specified. On one hand, the analysis concludes that there are no differences between firms according to the type of ownership, but on the other hand tariffs are higher in inland provinces due to a greater number of state-owned enterprises. Thus, the conclusion is not clear. Several hypotheses should be studied: some of the regions with low tariffs are not very industrialized, like Yunnan. What is the repartition of heavy industries? There are also value chains on the domestic markets because of the cost differences. The case of Xinjiang may be a result of political considerations. So, the explanations should be thorough.Third, the proportion of firms with zero tariffs is significantly higher in the group of foreign-owned firms. To have a better understanding of this result, a deeper investigation could be conducted on these questions: Did FDI between China and the United States increase to avoid the tariffs? Did China invest in other Asian countries to avoid tariffs? Did China shift some purchase of foreign goods away from the United States? Is China diversifying toward other suppliers?It could be suggested to look at the results in terms of trade volume and to address the complex issue of decoupling.The objectives of the tariffs from the United States were to increase U.S. exports and decrease the trade deficit. The duties imposed on 15 December 2019 have been cancelled because of the announcement of the Phase One agreement. Nevertheless, U.S. exports to China in 2022 reached only 59 percent of the second-year commitments (Bown and Wang 2023).U.S. imports goods from China has been reduced by the trade war; after four years of tariffs, China was the source of only 18 percent of total U.S. goods imports (22 percent before) (Bown 2022). On the contrary, U.S. imports from the rest of the world were 38 percent higher. In addition to overall figures, it is important to analyze geographical distribution, considering China's ability to use intermediate countries to penetrate the U.S. market. For instance, the U.S. imports of furniture from China decreased but they increased coming from Vietnam and Mexico. China relocated some productions in Vietnam to avoid tariffs. Mexico seems to be the winner of these tensions. Its imports from China are growing and it is now the first trade partner of the United States.U.S. imports are surging for some Chinese products never hit with tariffs, such as laptops and computer monitors, phones, video games consoles or toys (Bown 2022). At the present time, the decoupling between China and the United States concerns in particular high-tech products, not consumers goods. Then, trade war tariffs affected imports, but the question of decoupling is more complicated than the question of trade volume. There are many drivers of decoupling: research of diversification, self-reliance and national security for China, national security and reaction to the challenge posed by China for the United States (European Chamber of Commerce in China and MERICS 2021).One of the paper's proposals is that fostering cooperation is crucial in addressing the ongoing trade conflict. This is reasonable. Nevertheless, this does not prevent fragmentation and decoupling. Indirect effects can be significant. For instance, in May 2024 the United States announced that they are quadrupling tariffs on imported vehicles (from 25 percent to 100 percent) from China even though Chinese manufacturers have little presence on the American market. Of course, it could be a protection for the future of American automakers. But “by raising prices, the tariffs undermine the Biden administration's stated goals of reducing carbon emissions” (Packard 2024).Then, it is more and more based on strategic and political considerations. For Henry Paulson (2023), who served as the Secretary of the Treasury in the Bush administration, America's China policy is not working. He considers that “China and the United States are in a headlong descent from a competitive but sometimes cooperative relationship to one that is confrontational in nearly every respect.”The joint results of trade tariffs, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the Ukraine–Russia war are reflected in changes to the organization of global value chains and new forms of fragmentation. Trends toward decoupling will increase in the future, altering the impact of trade policies.
summary_html:
Main argument: This paper analyzes China's retaliatory tariffs during the U.S.-China trade war, focusing on tariff pass-through at the firm level within China. It argues that China adopted a cautious, strategically differentiated tariff policy to mitigate domestic economic costs while targeting U.S. exports, particularly avoiding tariffs on intermediate goods and high-technology sectors like semiconductors.

Research design: The study examines the differential distribution of retaliatory tariffs across Chinese firms and product categories to assess the economic and political logic underpinning tariff imposition, comparing these results with U.S. tariff strategies to highlight asymmetries and mutual strategic considerations.

Method: The authors use quantitative analysis of tariff pass-through to import prices and import volumes, focusing on heterogeneity by product classification, trade regime, firm ownership, regional location, and processing trade involvement.

Dataset or evidence: Firm-level Chinese import data capturing tariff rates, import values, and quantities during the trade war period, alongside comparative data on U.S. tariffs and trade flows. The study references secondary sources for contextualization, including trade volume shifts and tariff policy announcements.

Unit of analysis: Chinese importing firms, product categories, and regional units within China.

Time period studied: Primarily the trade war years up to and including 2020, with some reference to developments through 2022 and early 2024.

Geographic focus: China and, secondarily, the United States. Regional variation within China is also considered.

Identification strategy: The paper identifies tariff pass-through effects through firm-level variation in tariff exposure, isolating changes in import value and quantity corresponding to tariff increases. It leverages heterogeneity across firms, products, and regions to infer strategic policy considerations.

Key findings: A 10 percent increase in Chinese import duties on U.S. products correlates with a 2.75 percent drop in import value and a 1.51 percent decline in import quantity. Firms more involved in processing trade face lower tariffs. Tariffs vary by geographic region, with southeastern provinces facing lower rates. Tariffs are strategically targeted, avoiding intermediate goods and key high-tech sectors. U.S. tariffs aim principally at China’s high-tech exports, while China’s retaliation is more cautious, reflecting its processing trade reliance. The trade war induces partial decoupling, with shifts in supply chains toward third countries and mixed sectoral impacts.

Main limitations: The paper acknowledges the need for further causal inference on the role of firm ownership and regional industrial composition. It calls for deeper investigation into foreign direct investment shifts, supply chain relocation, and trade volume changes post-tariff. Historical and broader geopolitical contexts are not deeply integrated, limiting explanatory depth on strategic motivations and long-term impacts.

Why this matters for IR scholars: The analysis elucidates how economic tools like tariffs serve as instruments in geopolitical competition, showcasing the interplay between domestic economic structures and international strategic rivalry. It highlights the complexity of trade wars beyond simple protectionism, revealing nuanced firm-level and sectoral responses embedded in broader power competition dynamics.

Why this matters for strategic infrastructure research: The paper’s focus on tariff impacts in high-technology and intermediate goods sectors directly relates to strategic considerations in technological competition and supply chain resilience. Understanding China’s selective tariff strategy informs analyses of industrial policy, compute power supply chains, and the early signs of decoupling critical to AI governance and great power competition.

title: The US strategy of multidomain containment and China’s counter-responses in the Indo-Pacific (2019–2025)
abstract: Type of the article: Research articleThe intensifying United States-China rivalry in the Indo-Pacific has gained acute relevance for global order as strategic competition extends across military, technological, economic, and cognitive domains. This paper examines the extent and modalities of the US multidimensional strategic encirclement of China in the Indo-Pacific and analyzes China’s multidomain responses, including the PLA’s intelligentization, technological sovereignty initiatives, and economic re-sovereignization, over the period 2019–2025. The study adopts a qualitative interpretivist methodology, drawing on scholarly and primary sources, including defense doctrines, alliance frameworks such as AUKUS and QUAD, legislative instruments, and multilingual Chinese perspectives. The analysis shows that the US employs layered alliance-building, technology governance through semiconductor and export-control regimes, triangulated partnerships with actors such as Israel and India, and selective interventions in regional states, including Pakistan and the Philippines, to constrain Chinese influence. China’s countermeasures are multidimensional: advancing AI-enabled military modernization, securing strategic port access at Gwadar, Hambantota, and Ream, and reinforcing economic insulation through its Dual Circulation Strategy and yuan-based energy agreements. Results indicate that encirclement is no longer limited to geography but increasingly embedded in digital infrastructure, economic flows, and cognitive influence. The study concludes that these dynamics are accelerating a shift toward bifurcated multipolarity, marked by competing techno-security ecosystems and divergent governance norms, with significant implications for alliance cohesion, technological sovereignty, and the management of strategic escalation.Acknowledgments I would like to express my sincere gratitude to my teachers and academic peers whose valuable insights, encouragement, and constructive discussions inspire me to enrich the quality of my work. I am especially indebted to my family – my wife and children – for their patience, understanding, and unwavering support during the long hours of research and writing. Their endurance and encouragement made this endeavor possible.

INTRODUCTION
The rivalry between the United States and China in the Indo-Pacific 
has intensified into a multidomain contest that transcends tradi -
tional military confrontation. Since 2019, the Indo-Pacific has be -
come the principal arena in which the US seeks to operationalize a 
strategy of multidomain containment – integrating military deter -
rence, technological restrictions, economic coalitions, and norm a-
tive influence – to circumscribe China’s rise. The central pro blem 
that emerges is how this strategic encirclement is being constructed 
across multiple domains simultaneously, and to what extent it is re-
shaping the systemic balance of power. Rather than being confined 
to conventional geopolitical competition, the confrontation now e x-
tends into semiconductor supply chains, artificial intellige nce gover-
nance, alliance architectures, and the regulation of digital and eco -
nomic ecosystems.

This evolution creates a complex scientific problem for the study of international relations: understand-
ing how multidomain containment strategies are conceptualized and executed by a hegemon in relative 
decline, and how a rising power formulates adaptive counter-response s. Existing scholarship has ad -
dressed US hegemonic retrenchment (Ikenberry, 2008) and China’s ascent (Shambaugh, 2013), yet these 
works often isolate military deterrence from techno-economic rival ry or focus narrowly on decoupling 
debates. Such fragmentation obscures the interdependence of domains in which the rivalry unfolds and 
risks oversimplifying China’s strategic posture as merely reactive. The absence of an integrated, multi-
domain framework has resulted in blind spots in both policy assessment and aca demic analysis.
The problem under investigation, therefore, lies in the insufficiently theorized and empirically underde-
veloped understanding of how multidomain containment and counter-c ontainment strategies interact 
in real time in the Indo-Pacific between 2019 and 2025 (data collection cut- off: July 2025). Specifically, 
the challenge is to explain how alliance-building, doctrinal innovat ion, and indigenous technological 
development are mobilized in response to simultaneous pressures acro ss the military, economic, and 
technological theatres of competition. Addressing this problem is c rucial, as the period 2024–2025 has 
witnessed unprecedented intensification of semiconductor choke point strategies, artificial intelligence 
governance initiatives, and alliance expansion, all of which carry si gnificant implications for the future 
architecture of global order.
1. LITERATURE REVIEW
Scholarship on the US-China rivalry in the Indo-
Pacific has proliferated across several strands of 
international relations theory, yet remains frag -
mented in scope and integration. Three broad 
traditions – neorealism, offensive realism, and 
complex interdependence theory – provide the 
dominant conceptual frames for understand -
ing the dynamics of containment and counter-
containment. Neorealist scholarship highlights 
how systemic anarchy compels the US to engage 
in external balancing through alliance forma -
tion and forward deployment, a trend visible in 
AUKUS, the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue 
(QUAD), and renewed bilateral defense agree -
ments with India and Japan. These institution -
alized forms of balancing underscore how sys -
temic pressures generate collective responses to 
China’s rise. Building upon this, offensive real -
ism emphasizes the pursuit of regional hegemo -
ny: China’s assertive posture in the South China 
Sea, its Belt and Road Initiative, and its acceler -
ated military modernization are interpreted as 
steps toward displacing US primacy. US poli -
cies such as the 2022 Indo-Pacific Strategy (The 
White House, 2022) and the CHIPS and Science 
Act (Legislation of United States, 2022), which 
constrain Chinese technological growth, reflect 
pre-emptive containment measures rooted in 
hegemonic rivalry.
At the same time, realist interpretations are insuf -
ficient without recognition of economic and tech-
nological interdependence. Complex interdepen -
dence theory (Keohane & Nye, 1977) complicates 
zero-sum portrayals by illustrating how semicon -
ductor supply chains, rare earth dependencies, 
and cross-border financial flows bind the two ri -
vals even as these ties are weaponized. Export con-
trols imposed by Washington in 2022 and Beijing’s 
restrictions on gallium and germanium in 2023 
exemplify how interdependence has shifted from 
stabilizing linkage to a coercive instrument. The 
literature thus underscores a paradox: interdepen-
dence that once moderated conflict is now a con -
tested arena of statecraft.
Western scholarship has made substantial con -
tributions to theorizing this rivalry. Ikenberry 
(2008) and Friedberg (2011) conceptualize the 
Indo-Pacific contest as part of a liberal order un -
der stress, while Mearsheimer (2001) emphasizes 
the intensifying security dilemma. Recent analy -
ses highlight the convergence of deterrence and 
techno-economic denial (Glaser, 2015; Campbell 
& Doshi, 2025, yet often depict China as reactive 
rather than proactive. This tendency overlooks 
doctrinal developments such as the PLA’s intelli -
gentized warfare guidelines. Intelligentization  is 
an advanced integration of artificial intelligence, 
machine learning, data analytics, and cognitive 
computing into systems and structures, enabling 
47
Geopolitics under Globalization,  Volume 6, 2025
https://doi.org/10.21511/gg.06(1).2025.05
autonomous, adaptive, and intelligent opera -
tions that surpass traditional automation (Pan et 
al., 2024; State Council Information Office, 2019; 
Tellis, 2025), which frame technological inno -
vation as central to China’s strategic autonomy. 
Moreover, thematic compartmentalization per -
sists: works on military deterrence (Shambaugh, 
2013), economic decoupling (Baldwin, 2020), and 
technological bifurcation (Segal, 2016) remain an-
alytically siloed, obscuring the multidomain char -
acter of US containment.
Non-Western perspectives provide a more holistic 
understanding of the rivalry. Chinese scholarship, 
particularly through concepts such as major pow -
er diplomacy ( 大国外交), community of shared 
destiny ( 命运共同体), and intelligentized war -
fare ( 智能化战争), frames China’s rise as restor -
ative rather than revisionist. Yan Xuetong’s moral 
realism situates Chinese strategy in Confucian 
traditions and the tianxia worldview, while Liu 
Mingfu’s China Dream articulates a technologi -
cally empowered national rejuvenation. Regional 
voices from ASEAN emphasize inclusive order-
building, with the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-
Pacific (ASEAN, 2019) rejecting zero-sum for -
mulations. Singh and Marwah (2023) interpret 
China’s outreach as pragmatic balancing against 
what they perceive as Western conditionality. 
Similarly, national strategies from Japan, South 
Korea, India, and Australia reveal nuanced posi -
tions – ranging from Japan’s prioritization of AI 
and space security, to South Korea’s hedging be -
tween alliance commitments and economic ties, 
to India’s dual posture of alignment through the 
QUAD and strategic autonomy, and to Australia’s 
concern with “grey zone” coercion. The European 
Union, meanwhile, has advanced a normative 
Indo-Pacific agenda, with France and Germany 
participating in freedom of navigation operations 
(EU, 2021).
Across these literatures, three enduring contra -
dictions emerge. First, the stability–vulnerability 
paradox of interdependence highlights whether 
economic entanglement reduces or amplifies con-
flict risks. Second, competing interpretations of 
China’s intent divide the field: Western analyses 
tend to cast China as revisionist, whereas Chinese 
and some ASEAN perspectives emphasize restor -
ative and non-expansionist logics. Third, debates 
persist over whether military deterrence or tech -
no-economic leverage constitutes the primary are-
na of competition, with recent developments in AI 
governance and semiconductor control suggesting 
that the boundaries between the two are increas -
ingly blurred.
This review highlights the need for an integrated 
framework that synthesizes realist power-balanc -
ing, interdependence dynamics, and non-Western 
strategic thought. Existing studies, while rich in 
detail, often remain compartmentalized and epis -
temically asymmetric, privileging Western sourc -
es at the expense of Chinese primary materials. 
This study seeks to address these gaps by combin-
ing neorealism, offensive realism, and complex in-
terdependence with multilingual primary sources 
and underutilized Chinese strategic doctrines. In 
doing so, it contributes to a more comprehensive 
understanding of US multidomain containment 
and China’s counter-responses in the Indo-Pacific 
between 2019 and 2025, positioning this rivalry 
not merely as a geopolitical struggle but as a mul -
tidimensional contest over technology, alliances, 
and systemic order.
2. METHODS 
This study adopts a qualitative interpretive design 
to examine the dynamics of US multidomain con-
tainment and China’s counter-responses in the 
Indo-Pacific during the 2019 to 2025. The meth -
odological approach is structured in three stages: 
(1) corpus assembly, (2) data processing and cod -
ing, and (3) interpretive analysis.
2.1. Corpus assembly
The data set was purposively compiled to cap -
ture official strategy documents, legislative acts, 
alliance communiqués, peer-reviewed scholar -
ship, think tank reports, and reputable media 
analyses in both English and Chinese. Primary 
materials include China’s Defence White Papers 
(2020, 2023), the US Indo-Pacific Strategy (The 
White House, 2022), NATO Strategic Concepts 
(Vilnius 2022–2024), AUKUS and QUAD state -
ments, the CHIPS and Science Act, and policy 
papers from the Ministries of Foreign Affairs 
and Defence in China, the United States, and al -
48
Geopolitics under Globalization,  Volume 6, 2025
https://doi.org/10.21511/gg.06(1).2025.05
lied states. Supplementary sources were drawn 
from think tanks (e.g., CSIS, CNAS, Carnegie, 
Brookings; CIIS, SIIS, China Strategic Culture 
Promotion Association), peer-reviewed journals 
(International Security, China Quarterly, Foreign 
Affairs), and major regional and global media out-
lets (e.g., South China Morning Post, Financial 
Times, Global Times). Chinese-language docu -
ments were retrieved from PLA Daily ( 解放军报 
[pinyin: Jiěfàngjūn Bào]), Xinhua, and academic 
journals from institutions such as Renmin and 
Tsinghua Universities.
2.2. Data processing and coding
All textual data were imported into NVivo and 
Atlas.ti for thematic coding. An inductive code -
book was developed through open coding, followed 
by axial coding to identify cross-domain clusters, 
such as “containment,” “counter-containment,” 
“techno-sovereignty,” and “interdependence.” Co-
occurrence analysis was applied to detect relation-
ships between military, technological, and econom-
ic strategies. To ensure reliability, Chinese-language 
materials were processed through a two-stage pro-
cess to ensure both linguistic accuracy and concep-
tual fidelity. First, source texts were processed on 
encrypted, offline translation software, prevent -
ing any exposure of sensitive material to external 
servers. Second, translations were reviewed and 
refined by bilingual researchers with graduate-
level proficiency (C1 CEFR or equivalent) in the 
relevant languages and formal training in interna-
tional relations and security studies. For example, 
the Chinese doctrinal term “智能化战争” (zhìnéng 
huà zhànzhēng) was translated as “intelligentized 
warfare.” The alternatives such as “intelligent war-
fare” or “AI-enabled warfare,” were considered but 
retained “intelligentized warfare” to align with ter-
minology used in the People’s Liberation Army’s 
own white papers. 
2.3. Interpretive analysis
The study is grounded in constructivist episte -
mology, treating international strategy as socially 
constructed and ideologically framed. This inter -
pretive framework allows doctrinal statements, 
alliance structures, and policy narratives to be 
read not only as material instruments but also as 
discursive practices. The method complements 
the study’s theoretical synthesis of neorealism, of-
fensive realism, and complex interdependence, 
enabling analysis of both structural drivers (e.g., 
alliance-building, deterrence) and normative 
worldviews (e.g., “major power diplomacy,” “intel-
ligentized warfare”).
2.4. Ethical and practical 
considerations
All materials were derived from open-source and 
publicly available documents. The study follows 
COPE guidelines (2023), GDPR provisions, and 
China’s Personal Information Protection Law 
(2021). Personal identifiers in social media or com-
mentary sources were removed or anonymized. 
No IRB approval was required, as the study in -
volved no direct interaction with human partici -
pants. Where classified materials were unavail -
able, findings were triangulated with declassified 
documents, open-source intelligence (OSINT), 
and expert symposia. Interpretive neutrality was 
maintained through cross-checking ideologically 
divergent sources (e.g., Global Times vs. CSIS).
3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
This study examined the modalities of the United 
States’ multidomain containment strategy in the 
Indo-Pacific and China’s counter-responses be -
tween 2019 and 2025. Using interpretive thematic 
coding of multilingual primary and secondary 
sources, the findings reveal a layered and asym -
metrical rivalry unfolding across military, tech -
nological, economic, and ideational domains. This 
section integrates empirical results (Tables 1-8; 
Figures 1-2) with theoretical interpretation, there-
by situating the evidence within the hybrid frame-
work of neorealism, offensive realism, and com -
plex interdependence.
3.1. US encircling China
The data confirm that Washington’s strategy oper-
ates as a strategic mesh (Table 1), comprising over-
lapping alliances (AUKUS, QUAD, JAPHUS, NATO 
outreach) and techno-security nodes. This modular 
network is consistent with Mearsheimer’s offensive 
realism, which highlights the creation of redundant 
balancing mechanisms against rising challengers. 
49
Geopolitics under Globalization,  Volume 6, 2025
https://doi.org/10.21511/gg.06(1).2025.05
These networked frameworks follow what 
Mearsheimer (2001) would term offensive real -
ism in modular alliance formation, where the US 
hedges against China’s rise by building overlap -
ping technological and military dependencies in 
regions adjacent to China’s core maritime corri -
dors (e.g., South and East China Seas).
Yet, complex interdependence is also evident: 
India and Israel serve as intermediary hubs for 
technology transfers (Table 2), allowing the US to 
shape Asia’s defense ecosystem without triggering 
overt escalation.
These transfers align with the dual logic of real -
ist containment and neoliberal interdependence, 
whereby US retains control over core components 
while leveraging allied national champions to 
populate Asia’s defense-technological ecosystem.
NATO’s 2024 Vilnius Summit marks a notable se-
mantic shift in the Alliance’s doctrinal perimeter. 
By explicitly labelling China a “systemic challenge,” 
NATO moves beyond its traditional Atlantic focus, 
signalling a doctrinal convergence between Euro-
Atlantic and Indo-Pacific strategies (NATO, 2024). 
This evolution supports the argument that the en-
circlement is not just regional but systemic.
Western scholars often interpret this shift as ideo-
logical – liberal democracies reacting to authori -
tarian assertiveness (Ikenberry, 2008). However, 
Chinese analyses see it as “cognitive encirclement” 
(认知包围 [rènzhī bāowéi]), a term used in PLA 
Daily to describe the West’s effort to define Chinese 
intentions in adversarial terms (Pu et al., 2023).
The re-engagement with Pakistan (Table 3) illus -
trates a nuanced extension of containment through 
selective realignment. Coding patterns link “US-
Pakistan Engagement” with themes of “peripheral 
ambiguity,” suggesting that Washington is seek -
ing to dilute Beijing’s monopoly in South Asia 
without rupturing Islamabad’s ties to CPEC. This 
analytical finding refines Waltzian neorealism: al -
liances are built not only on systemic necessity but 
also on tactical flexibility and soft-power linkages.
While Western literature often dismisses Pakistan 
as a “swing state” with minimal autonomy (Fair, 
2018), Chinese defense scholars emphasize the 
geostrategic centrality of Pakistan as a “continen -
tal anchor” in Beijing’s BRI-maritime convergence 
strategy (Abb, 2023). This reveals the epistemic 
gap in strategic weighting between Western and 
Chinese analysts, which this research helps to 
reconcile.

posture. PLA modernization, shifting from mech-
anization to “intelligentization,” is reflected in in-
digenous R&D on hypersonic, drone swarms, and 
battlefield AI (Table 4). 
China’s “intelligentization” aligns with both 
Mearsheimer’s offensive realism and Keohane and 
Nye’s interdependence, as it reflects a state navi -
gating between strategic independence and tech -
nological entanglement – especially in AI systems 
where semiconductor dependency still exists.
Maritime infrastructure projects such as Gwadar, 
Hambantota, and Djibouti (Table 5) demonstrate 
Beijing’s ambition to secure extended naval supply 
lines, a direct challenge to US SLOC dominance.

3.5. Structured containment and 
asymmetric levers
Evidence from Tables 1-3 confirms that US con -
tainment operates as a multi-vector encirclement 
strategy. AUKUS and QUAD have evolved beyond 
diplomatic forums into AI-enabled defense archi -
tectures, extending deterrence into cyber and space 
domains. The India-Israel-US tech corridor exem-
plifies asymmetric control, allowing Washington to 
regulate dual-use transfers indirectly (Segal, 2016; 
CRS, 2023). Tactical re-engagements with Pakistan 
and ASEAN demonstrate selective realignment, an 
attempt to fracture China’s peripheral partnerships.
These findings align with Waltzian neorealism, 
where alliances reflect systemic necessity in an an-
archic order (Waltz, 1979), but the US emphasis 
on narrative framing (“democracy vs. autocracy”) 
suggests a constructivist layer. Atlas.ti co-occur -
rence maps under “Narrative Shaping” confirm 
this duality: material containment is reinforced by 
ideological legitimacy claims.
3.6. China’s proactive counter-
containment
Chinese strategies, as coded under “Proactive 
Counter-Containment,” demonstrate pre-emp -
tive adaptation rather than a reactive posture. The 
PLA’s intelligentization doctrine – R&D in hyper-
sonic, drone swarms, and battlefield AI (Table 4) – 
illustrates Beijing’s intent to achieve offensive parity. 
Maritime facilities from Gwadar to Djibouti (Table 
5) extend China’s deterrence footprint into blue-wa-
ter domains, countering US SLOC dominance.
The “Dual Circulation Strategy” (Table 6) signals 
selective decoupling, insulating critical sectors 
(semiconductors, yuan-based energy) while deep -
ening South–South technology partnerships with 
Russia and Iran. Atlas.ti co-occurrence analysis 
shows “Technological Sovereignty” bridging with 
“Narrative Rebalancing”, suggesting that capacity 
building and ideational repositioning are mutu -
ally reinforcing.
This behavior embodies offensive realism’s pow -
er-maximization logic but also resonates with 
complex interdependence theory (Keohane & 
Nye, 1977), since Beijing cannot fully detach from 
global supply chains. Thus, China emerges as both 
revisionist and status quo-conserving, depending 
on the domain.
3.7. Dual techno-security 
architectures
Results highlight the consolidation of two com -
peting yet interdependent techno-security eco -
systems (Table 8). The US relies on CHIPS Act re-
gimes, export controls, and Bretton Woods lever -
age; China emphasizes dual circulation, Huawei 
AI, and yuan-based trade networks. NVivo/Atlas.
ti bridging codes (“Selective Interdependence,” 
“Environmental Tech Cooperation”) confirm that 
decoupling remains compartmentalized, not 
absolute.
This finding complicates neorealist and offensive 
realist predictions of bipolar fracture. Instead, it 
validates complex interdependence theory: sys -
temic rivalry persists alongside selective collabo -
ration in domains such as climate technology and 
health governance.

3.9. Complex containment in  
a semi-anarchic order
Synthesizing across domains, the final axial cat -
egory “complex containment” emerges (Figures 
1-2). The US-China rivalry is neither a Cold War 
replay nor a simple hegemonic transition. Instead, 
it manifests as layered alliances, proxy trans -
fers, narrative contests, and compartmentalized 
interdependence.
• Neorealism explains the architecture of sys -
temic alliances.
• Offensive realism captures the logic of power 
maximization through forward deployments 
and technological insulation.
• Complex interdependence theory unpacks the 
paradox of simultaneous rivalry and coopera -
tion in high-tech, economic, and environmen-
tal arenas.
The methodological chain – NVivo hierarchies, 
Atlas.ti co-occurrence patterns, triangulated cod -
ing memos – ensures empirical grounding of in -
terpretive claims. The result is a theoretically inte-
grated and validated data analysis of Indo-Pacific 
rivalry as semi-anarchic complex containment, 
where both powers are simultaneously decoupling 
and entangling, deterring and cooperating.
This architecture challenges the binarism of classic 
IR theories. While neorealism and offensive real -
ism explain the security dilemma logic, they fail to 
capture the hybrid interdependence that persists in 
digital, environmental, and health domains. Hence, 
complex interdependence theory (Keohane & Nye, 
1977) is necessary to fill in the explanatory gaps.
The analysis, using Atlas.ti, revealed two dense 
thematic clusters: “US-led Network” and “China-
led Network”, linked by bridging codes such as 
“Selective Interdependence” and “Environmental 
Tech Cooperation.” The evidence-based existence 
of bridging codes supports the complex interdepen-
dence theory of Keohane and Nye (1977), showing 
that complete decoupling is neither occurring nor 
feasible – filling the literature gap on domain-specif-
ic cooperation in competitive contexts.
However, as with comparable qualitative interpre-
tive studies in international relations (e.g., Yan, 
2019; Farrell & Newman, 2019), this paper is sub -
ject to several limitations. First, reliance on open-
source and declassified materials means that clas -
sified strategic deliberations remain outside the 
scope of analysis. Second, while Chinese-language 
materials were processed through a semantic 
translation pipeline and verified, subtle linguis -
tic or cultural nuances may not be fully captured. 
Third, the temporal boundary of the study (2019–
2025) restricts generalization to subsequent devel-
opments. Finally, interpretive coding inevitably

CONCLUSION
The purpose of this study was to examine the extent and modalities of the United S tates’ multido-
main containment strategy toward China in the Indo-Pacific between 2019 a nd 2025, and to ana -
lyze China’s multidimensional counter-responses. By combining ne orealism, offensive realism, and 
complex interdependence within an interpretive qualitative desi gn, the research traced how alli -
ance expansion, techno-economic rivalry, and ideational contest ation interact in shaping regional 
security dynamics.
The analysis demonstrates that the US strategy is best understood as a struct ured containment 
framework, anchored in alliance institutionalization (AUKUS, QU AD, NATO Indo-Pacific fram -
ing), technology-denial regimes (CHIPS Act, AI export controls), an d selective realignments on 
China’s periphery. China’s response is not merely reactive, but reflect s a proactive counter-con -
tainment posture, evident in PLA intelligentization, dual circula tion economic insulation, yuan-
based trade settlements, and narrative reframing around developme ntal pluralism and community 
of shared future. Together, these processes produce a dual techno-secu rity architecture (Table 8), 
marked by selective decoupling in strategic technologies but continu ed interdependence in envi -
ronmental, health, and economic domains.
From these findings, three conclusions emerge. First, the Indo-Pacifi c rivalry cannot be reduced to 
Cold War analogies; rather, it reflects a form of complex containment, whe re decoupling and en -
tanglement coexist (Figures 1-2). Second, containment and counter -containment operate not only 
through military positioning but also through narrative shaping and di gital-technical ecosystems, 
underscoring the need for multidomain analysis. Third, the persistenc e of bridging codes such as 
“Selective Interdependence” confirms that rivalry is structurally e mbedded yet institutionally me -
diated, suggesting that the system is competitive but not ungoverned.
Future research should test the durability of this complex containmen t framework in the face of 
AI-driven military innovation, semiconductor chokepoints, and s hifting alliance dynamics after 
2025. Comparative work incorporating Russian, ASEAN, and E U perspectives could expand the 
model’s explanatory reach, while longitudinal studies on AI go vernance and economic securitiza -
tion could assess whether selective interdependence stabilizes or d estabilizes regional order.
By integrating theory, method, and evidence, this study contribute s to the international relations 
literature by offering a hybrid conceptualization of Indo-Pacific riv alry as semi-anarchic, multido -
main containment. It equips scholars with a framework for understandin g systemic transforma -
tion and provides policymakers with analytical tools to anticipate bot h the risks and opportunities 
of US-China strategic competition in an interdependent yet adversar ial era.

Main argument: The paper argues that the US adopts a multidomain containment strategy against China in the Indo-Pacific from 2019 to 2025, integrating military, technological, economic, and cognitive tools to encircle China strategically. In response, China pursues proactive multidomain countermeasures including military "intelligentization," technological sovereignty, and economic insulation, resulting in a layered rivalry that transcends traditional geopolitical boundaries and fosters a bifurcated multipolar order defined by competing techno-security ecosystems and governance norms.

Research design: This is a qualitative interpretivist research design combining theoretical synthesis of neorealism, offensive realism, and complex interdependence theory with an empirical analysis of primary and secondary multilingual sources to develop an integrative framework explaining the multidomain US containment and Chinese counter-containment interaction.

Method: The study uses qualitative interpretive analysis conducted in three stages: corpus assembly of multilingual primary and secondary texts, thematic coding using NVivo and Atlas.ti, and interpretive triangulation. It involves inductive and axial coding, co-occurrence and network analysis, and cross-checking between ideologically divergent sources to ensure conceptual reliability and epistemic balance.

Dataset or evidence: The dataset consists of official strategy and defense documents (e.g., US Indo-Pacific Strategy, China Defense White Papers), alliance communiqués (AUKUS, QUAD, NATO), legislative acts (CHIPS Act), primary Chinese-language materials (PLA Daily, CIIS reports), think tank reports, peer-reviewed scholarship, and regional/global media outlets. It includes 41 references, 2 figures, and 8 tables documenting alliance structures, technology transfers, and economic initiatives.

Unit of analysis: The unit of analysis is state-level strategic interaction between the United States and China within the Indo-Pacific region, focusing on multidomain (military, technological, economic, cognitive) containment and counter-containment strategies and the institutions, narratives, and networks underpinning this rivalry.

Time period studied: The study covers 2019 to 2025, with data collection cut off in July 2025, capturing the intensification of US-China competition, especially in semiconductor governance, AI military innovation, and alliance-building developments.

Geographic focus: The primary geographic focus is the Indo-Pacific region, including peripheral states such as Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, and maritime chokepoints important for naval and commercial access. The study also considers global alliance networks extending to transatlantic actors like NATO.

Identification strategy: Identification relies on triangulated interpretive analysis of official and secondary documents in multiple languages, combined with thematic coding to detect multidomain strategy patterns and narratives. Epistemic rigor is ensured via bilingual expert validation of translations and cross-validation of contesting ideological perspectives.

Key findings: The US employs a "strategic mesh" of overlapping alliances (AUKUS, QUAD, NATO Indo-Pacific outreach), technology denial regimes (CHIPS Act, export controls), and selective peripheral realignments (e.g., Pakistan, Philippines) with ideological framing of liberal democracy versus authoritarianism. China counters with AI-enabled military modernization, expansion of overseas maritime infrastructure (string of pearls), and economic policies promoting technological sovereignty and yuan-based trade. The rivalry evolves into competing techno-security ecosystems characterized by selective decoupling and persistent interdependence in some domains. Ideational narratives diverge sharply, with the US emphasizing a rules-based liberal order and China promoting developmental pluralism and South-South cooperation.

Main limitations: The study is limited by reliance on open-source and declassified materials excluding classified deliberations, potential translation and cultural nuance challenges in Chinese-language sources, temporal restriction to 2019–2025 limiting post-2025 applicability, and inherent subjectivity in qualitative interpretive coding despite methodological safeguards.

Why this matters for IR scholars: This paper advances IR scholarship by integrating multiple theoretical paradigms and linguistic/cultural perspectives to capture the complex multidomain nature of great power competition beyond traditional military or economic silos. It challenges simplistic bipolar or decoupling frameworks and highlights how narrative construction and techno-economic entanglements reshape alliance and rivalry dynamics, offering a nuanced lens to study emerging multipolarity and techno-political order transformation.

Why this matters for strategic infrastructure research: The study is strategically critical as it maps how semiconductor geopolitics, AI-enabled military innovation, and economic infrastructure investments underpin the US-China rivalry. It reveals how strategic infrastructure—ports, semiconductor supply chains, AI governance frameworks—is weaponized to secure technological sovereignty and influence regional order, providing vital insights for policymakers and scholars focused on technological competition, industrial policy, and the geopolitics of critical infrastructure security in a digitally interconnected yet adversarial international environment.

title: The Economy–Security Nexus: Risk, Strategic Autonomy and the Regulation of the Semiconductor Supply Chain
abstract: Abstract The EU’s policies in the field of technology broadly defined are increasingly marked by a concern over strategic autonomy, and Europe’s place in the world. Regulatory interventions are framed in terms of “digital sovereignty,” with the Commission seeking to ensure that external dependencies are reduced with the aim of increasing the EU’s resilience to geopolitical instability and external shocks. Using the case study of semiconductors, the chips that power modern electronic devices, this article explores how technology policy in the EU sits at the economy–security nexus, in which economic goals and security goals are interdependent and inseparable. Focusing on the life cycle of the semiconductor supply chain from the control over natural resources through to the cybersecurity requirements placed on the finished products, this article demonstrates the increasing security logic embedded within a burgeoning industrial technology policy.

ARTICLE
The Economy –Security Nexus: Risk, Strategic
Autonomy and the Regulation of the Semiconductor
Supply Chain
Benjamin Farrand
Newcastle Law School, Newcastle University, Newcastle-Upon-Tyne, UK
Email: ben.farrand@ncl.ac.uk
Abstract
The EU ’s policies in the field of technology broadly defined are increasingly marked by a concern
over strategic autonomy, and Europe ’s place in the world. Regulatory interventions are framed in
terms of “digital sovereignty, ” with the Commission seeking to ensure that external dependencies
are reduced with the aim of increasing the EU ’s resilience to geopolitical instability and external
shocks. Using the case study of semiconductors, the chips that power modern electronic devices, this
article explores how technology policy in the EU sits at the economy –security nexus, in which
economic goals and security goals are interdependent and inseparable. Focusing on the life cycle of
the semiconductor supply chain from the control over natural resources through to the
cybersecurity requirements placed on the finished products, this article demonstrates the increasing
security logic embedded within a burgeoning industrial technology policy.
Keywords: digital sovereignty ; security; semiconductors; strategic autonomy
I. Introduction
“Digital is the make-or-break issue [and] there is no digital without chips. ”1 Such was the
pronouncement of Commission President von der Leyen at the 2021 EU State of the Union.
EU digital policies have increasingly moved away from a binary between economy-and-
internal market initiatives on the one hand, and cybersecurity initiatives on the other. The
Union has seen itself increasingly beset by a range of geopolitical instabilities and global
shocks, from pandemic to conflict on its borders. Its place in the world, and its responses to
these insecurities, have resulted in a more assertive agenda, moving from traditional
liberal economic approaches to approaches based in the merging of economic and security
goals. The EU ’s “strategic autonomy, ” its ability to act independently and free of
dependencies upon external actors, has expanded beyond military and defence issues to
become its response to global upheaval generally, as a response to great-power rivalries
reemerging, technological disruptions and the increasing use of leveraged interdepen-
dence,
2 in trade as much as in war. Semiconductors, the chips that power all modern

exploring these dynamics, identifying the ways in which economic concerns and security
concerns are brought together, justifying increased regulation on the basis of preserving
and furthering strategic autonomy. This article takes an approach of considering the
regulation of the semiconductor supply chain, from the harvesting of raw materials,
through the research and design, manufacture, and use of these critical components. It
demonstrates the economy-security nexus in EU digital policy, and how strategic
autonomy as much as market integration, serves as a basis for the furthering of EU laws in
technology sectors. In doing so, it serves to make a broader, generalisable case about the
EU as a geopolitical actor that goes beyond the immediate case study.
II. Semiconductors, geopolitical vulnerability and strategic autonomy
In considering the merging of security and economic concerns and goals in technology
governance, it is useful to begin with some definitions and explanations of the interrelated
technologies at the centre of this article ’s analysis. The first is semiconductors.
Semiconductors are materials with the capacity to conduct electricity at a value between
that of traditional conductive metals such as silver or copper, and traditional insulators,
such as glass (and thus have electrical resistivity above those conductors, but below that of
insulators).
3 Semiconductors are useful insofar as their electrical conductivity increases
with heat, rather than decreasing as traditional metal conductors do. 4 In terms of materials
relevant for the microprocessor industry, the two most important semiconductors are
silicon and germanium as “elemental” semiconductors, upon which the commercial
processor markets depend.
5 Central to their function is their crystalline structure, which
allows for reproduction at an atomic level of their lattice composition. 6 Ultimately,
semiconductors are materials that have properties that make them essential; they are the
key component in microchips, which power all modern electronics, from fridges to cars,
smartphones to autonomous weapons systems. Microchips are generally described in
terms of the number of transistors on a chip. The number of transistors on a chip can
number in the millions or even billions – this of course requires they are incredibly small,
nanometres (nm) in size. Therefore, the smaller the semiconductor transistor, the more
can fit on a chip, and the more advanced the processing that the chip can perform.
“Commodity” chips tend have transistors larger than 7nm in size (and thus less can fit on a
single chip), whereas high-end processing in advanced fields of computing use chips with
transistors smaller than 7nm in size, with chips as small as 3nm becoming available in
2022, allowing for far greater computational capacity.
7
The above discussion also helps to highlight why semiconductors, and by extension
chips, are important. In the 21 st Century, our lives are dependent upon chips. This is not
hyperbole – microchips are integrated into technologies that provide water sanitisation
and electricity delivery, power our medical technologies and agricultural systems, connect
us in our social and professional lives, and equip our security and defence systems.

III. Regulation at the beginning of the chain: Securing strategic natural
resources
The first aspect of the semiconductor supply chain to consider is the security of the natural
resources from which microprocessors are built. As discussed in the preceding section,
these chips require the chemical elements silicon, gallium and germanium to act as
semiconductors to be able to function. The EU finds itself heavily dependent on other
countries for its supply of these materials, and as such is highly vulnerable to market
shocks,
28 impacting upon its strategic autonomy. Geopolitically, this is a concern for the EU
as 71% of the world ’s silicon, 80% of its germanium, and 98% of its gallium is processed in
China,29 and the EU relies upon China for 11% of its silicon and 27% of its gallium imports,
while being dependent on imports from outside the EU for 63% of its silicon, 31% of its
gallium, and 100% of its lithium, which is also required for chip production.
30 The EU has
described these vulnerabilities in explicit security terms, stating that they are central to its
economic, trade, and security interests
31 and highlighting that access to these critical raw
resources is necessary for its economic competitiveness 32 and the functioning of its
defence industries. 33
The focus of regulation in this field is in securing the resilience of these supply chains to
guarantee European access, as well as fostering relations with third countries that are key
producers of desired resources. In 2023, the Commission published a Communication on a
secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials,
34 in which it framed the security of
these supply chains as essential for its strategic autonomy. It proposed that its actions in
the field should include reducing single-country dependencies for resources (thereby
diversifying its supply chains), increase self-sufficiency through domestic production of
critical materials where possible, and adopt a global leadership position through
establishing partnerships with third countries that would serve to boost their economies
while securing access to their resources for the EU.
35 The Commission subsequently
published a Proposal for a Regulation on Critical Raw Materials, 36 which highlighted that
the aim of this legislation would be to guarantee resources important to the European
economy, framing this in terms of the geopolitical security risks that could potentially
threaten supply chains.
